124	A - the stage of the concentrated loads; ti - duration of this stage;
125	B - the stage of the specific training loads with the gradual increase of their intensity; U - duration of this stage; 
126	Curves fi, U and fs - the three possible variants of the athlete’s body response to the training loads influence 
127	through the change of the functional parameters level (f).
128	525
129	
130	===== PDF 537 / p.526 =====
131	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
132	ity and an objective prerequisite in a rational system of high level athlete preparation. Purposeful 
133	creation of conditions for bringing about purposefully directed use of LDTE of concentrated 
134	loads, opens up wide and still little used, possibilities for increasing the effectiveness of the train­
135	ing process in the yearly cycle of preparation (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25).
136	Figure 8 - Dynamics of the speed-strength parameters, the volumes of the carried out training loads and the sport 
137	results of the triple jumper during the yearly cycle (from October - to August):
138	On the graphic above - the level of the speed-strength parameters evaluated every month:
139	P0, maximal strength,
140	Fmax, magnitude of the maximal explosive effort,
141	- 
142	J<j., index of explosive strength 
143	On the graphic in low - the total volume of different training loads carried out in every month: 
144	barbell exercises (in tones - on the left axe);
145	bounds - the total distance which was overcame in bounds (in km - on the rigth axe); 
146	the whole competition exercises executions (number of repetitions - on the left axe).
147	On the graphic in the middle - the results of the competition exercise execution (triple jump).
148	526
149	
150	===== PDF 538 / p.527 =====
151	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
152	Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation 
153	of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide 
154	moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or an­
155	other functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reac­
156	tions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body.
157	The reason for such happenings is tied in with the changes in the external interactions of the 
158	body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mas­
159	tery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, 
160	and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakov­
161	lev, 144 ).
162	There are three levels of adaptation restructuring, each of which has its own specific character in 
163	regard to heterochronicity of the accommodating restructuring and their corresponding physio­
164	logical processes and structural transformation (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky, 
165	Viru.28, 286 ).
166	1.6. 
167	H etero ch ro n ism o f the a d a p ta tio n a l re s tru c tu rin g
168	Figure 9 - The sequence of the reparative biosynthesises in the muscles during the work and recovery (N. Yakov­
169	lev, 1986)
170	527
171	
172	===== PDF 539 / p.528 =====
173	SUPERTR.AINING ADDENDUM
174	They are:
175	level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and 
176	immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions); 
177	level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the 
178	structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation); 
179	level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation).
180	On the first level there are fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecu­
181	tiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9).
182	In work, there is high excitation energy necessary for the muscle work and in the post work pe­
183	riod. liquidation of the biochemical changes that have taken place in the muscles and other or­
184	gans during the time of muscular work.
185	The most expressed changes are observed in energy exchange. In the muscle work there is a de­
186	crease in the content of the substrates for energy conversion (creatine phosphate, glycogen, and 
187	during long term work even the lipids) and an increase in the content of intercellular metabolism 
188	products.
189	The accumulation of these products and the stronger hormonal activity stimulates the oxidative 
190	processes in the tissues in the rest period after work. This serves to restore the intramuscular re­
191	serve of energy products, which leads to normalization of the water-electrolyte balance of the 
192	body and ensures the inductive synthesis of proteins in the organs that were subjected to the 
193	loads (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38).
194	The process of restoration, during the period of rest after muscular work, takes place at different 
195	speeds and ends at different times (Table 2).
196	TABLE 2 - Time necessary for restoration of different biochemical processes in the period of rest after loaded muscle 
197	work (According to N. Volkov. 1986 and E. Fox, 1981)
198	Restorative Process
199	Time of restoration
200	Restoration of the phosphogens in the muscles (ATP and CP)
201	From 2-3 min
202	Restoration of oxygen reserves in the body
203	From 10-15 sec.
204	Payback/recovery of alactic oxygen debt
205	From 3-5 min
206	Clearance of lactic acid:
207	- in conditions of active rest
208	- in conditions of passive rest
209	From 30 min to 1 hour 
210	From 1-2 hr.
211	Restoration of inter muscular reserves of glycogen:
212	- after long term work
213	- after non long term work
214	From 10-46 hours 
215	From 5-24 hours
216	Restoration of glycogen reserves in the liver
217	From 12-48 hours
218	Strengthening of inductive synthesis of enzyme and structural 
219	proteins
220	From 12-72 hours
221	528
222	
223	===== PDF 540 / p.529 =====
224	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
225	Oxygen reserves and creatine phosphate in the working muscles are the fastest to recover fol­
226	lowed by inter muscular reserves of glycogen and liver glycogen and then the fat reserves that 
227	were used up during the protein structure work.
228	It is known that the intensity of the flow of the restorative processes, and the periods of filling 
229	the energy reserves in the body, depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure dur­
230	ing the time of muscular work (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38).
231	In the formation of compensatory accustomization restructuring, a definite consecutiveness in the 
232	improvement of physiological factors that determine the working effect of the motor functions 
233	can be clearly seen (Verkhoshansky 17, 24, 281- 284).
234	In a loaded work regime a shift in the 
235	functional characteristics of the body is 
236	observed first (Figure 10).
237	Intensification of this function acti­
238	vates a corresponding morphological 
239	(structural) restructuring (2), which, 
240	comes out as a quality material base 
241	for the adaptation process. This makes 
242	it possible to get further intensification 
243	of this function. Development of these 
244	mutually conditioning processes in 
245	turn, creates the prerequisites for rais­
246	ing the effect (power) of the external 
247	work of the body, which is reached by 
248	the more complete realization o f the 
249	motor potential of the body (Verkho­
250	shansky, 26, 27, 283, 284).
251	On the global level of the functional 
252	systemic restructuring of the body, development of adaptational changes are realized first of all 
253	because of the improved strength of the bio energetic processes. Following this is the bio energy 
254	volume and finally, improved bioenergetic effectiveness (economy) characterized by the level of 
255	use of the released energy into the metabolic processes for execution of specific muscle work.
256	In relation to separate bio energetic systems, the consecutiveness of development of adaptation 
257	during training takes on the following form: a faster increase in the capability of the aerobic oxi­
258	dative processes and maintenance of glycogen in the working muscles. Following this is mainte­
259	nance of the myofibril proteins (actin and myosin) and intensity of glycolosis. At the end, after 
260	everything - is maintenance of creatine phosphate (CP) and activeness of the creatine phos- 
261	phokinasis in the muscles (Margaria et al, 242, Yakovlev, 144, Volkov 38).
262	In this way, we get the greatest tempo of development and a longer period of maintaining a 
263	maximally high level that is characteristic for the biochemical indices of endurance for long term 
264	work, i.e., the aerobic abilities of the athlete. There is significantly slower development and 
265	shorter maintenance of a maximally high level of the biochemical indices of speed-strength 
266	qualities and speed endurance (Volkov, 38, Yakovlev, 144).
267	Several aspects of the heterochronicity phenomena of adaptation restructuring will be looked at 
268	further on in the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization of the athlete's body.
269	529
270	
271	===== PDF 541 / p.530 =====
272	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
273	In the process of forming the behavioral adaptation reactions during strenuous muscle activity 
274	with complex motor coordination, attention is first given to the economically wasteful generali­
275	zation phase. This is seen in an abundance of extra movements in generally constrained move­
276	ments, motor system errors and a sharply expressed vegetative component (Bernstein. 7). Further 
277	on, according to the amount of skill formation and consolidation of extra movements in the mo­
278	tor system errors are eliminated and the vegetative component of the reaction is significantly de­
279	creased. In this way the end result becomes sufficient for maximum economy of the body re­
280	sources (Bernstein, 7, Farfel, 120, Verkhoshansky, 17, 25, 281, 281, Person, 95, 96, Donskoy, 
281	50, Granit, 210).
282	In this way, during successful adaptation to very different factors in the environment, high func­
283	tional economy appears to be a general characteristic trait of the systems, responsible for the ad­
284	aptation. This trait appears on different level of the system activity' as follows:
285	- 
286	on both the cellular and organ levels, where it is determined by the ratio of the different cel­
287	lular structures involved in the adaptive response;
288	on the level of the systems as a whole, where it is determined by the ratio of different or­
289	gans; and finally
290	on the level of neuro-humoral regulation, where economy appears as a consequence of 
291	greater reactiveness of the adapted organs to the mediator and hormone actions (Meerson, 
292	77, Viru, Kirge, 35, Haydarliu, 124).
293	One of the indicators of the athlete's adaptation to physical loads appears to be economy of the 
294	physiological systems functioning at rest and during moderate, sub-maximal loads. At the same 
295	time, during maximum loads, the body is capable of achieving a level of system functioning 
296	which is not possible by the untrained body (Farfel, 120, Pshennikova, 99). This feature is seen 
297	both within the limits of compensation as well as in the results of long term adaptation (Verkho­
298	shansky, Viru. 28. 286).
299	For example, the schematic on Figure 11 shows that doing low power work is easy for both the 
300	trained and untrained person, as differences in the physiological shifts (changes in energy expen­
301	diture, minute blood volume, breathing fre­
302	quency, etc.) are hardly seen. In more in­
303	tense work, in the untrained, a more sub­
304	stantial physiological shift takes place than 
305	in the trained, and with increases in the 
306	loads 
307	these 
308	differences 
309	become 
310	even 
311	greater.
312	When work is given that is maximal for the 
313	untrained, the functional shifts in them 
314	reach maximum, but in the trained they are 
315	still moderate, that is, for them this work is 
316	comparatively not hard.
317	The trained athlete can accomplish work
318	1.7. 
319	F u n ctio n al econom y o f the a d a p te d body
320	530
321	
322	===== PDF 542 / p.531 =====
323	SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
324	with intensities that are significantly higher than those, wrhich for the untrained, appear to be 
325	maximal. In this, corresponding physiological shifts continue to increase. In the end, it reaches a 
326	limit work intensity and at this moment for the trained athletes it registers a maximum functional 
327	shift (Pshennicova, 99).
328	Means of economizing body functions during loaded muscle activity are extremely diverse and 
329	are determined by the functional specifics of the life ensuring systems of the body.
330	For example, in adaptation to loaded muscular activity requiring endurance, a significant in­
331	crease in the number of mitochondria in the skeletal muscles leads to a state that when at rest, or 
332	when the muscles are loaded, the portion of oxygen extracted from each liter of the flowing 
333	blood is greater than in the untrained body. As a result, an extreme increase in the minute volume 
334	of the heart during loaded activity shows up as being superfluous and ensures economy of blood 
335	circulation (Pshennikova, 99). Together with this, an increase in the strength of the mitochondrial 
336	system serves to increase the intensity of pyruvate utilization, decreasing its transition to lactate 
337	and consequently less accumulation of lactate in the muscles (Morgan et al., 250, Hollocszy, 
338	219, Riedy et al, 259).
339	In the end, the increased aerobic power of the body leads to an increase in its ability to utilize 
340	lipids to provide energy. The lipids have less of an energy effect in comparison to carbohydrates, 
341	but apparently they are used as a quality substrate for oxidation, sharply increasing the amount of 
342	energy as a consequence of their practically inexhaustible supply (Yakovlev, 140. Panin, 94,

This stage ensures a sufficiently long period of preparation during which the organs and systems 
can respond to the physiological loads faster and more significantly activate biosynthesis and 
correspondingly, faster formation of the needed structures. These changes are much greater than 
can be produced in conditions of sharp loads in the absence of an increased fund of prepared ri­
bosomes and increased activity of the entire protein-synthesizing apparatus (Meerson, 76).
Even before this it had been shown that in the process of physical work, the biochemical shifts 
that take place in the body during the period of rest become normalized, going through a series of 
phases which include the phase of supercompensation of those ingredients that were expended. 
This pertains to the substrates serving as sources of energy as well as the different structural and 
enzymatic proteins (Yakovlev, 138).
For example, the content of glycogen

Thus after work, during the time of 
rest, not only is the pre-work state of 
the muscles restored (and the body as 
a whole) but for some period, condi­
tions for increased workability are 
created. In this, the amount of super- 
compensation and the speed of its appearance, is directly related to the intensity of the expended 
products during the time of work, and the duration of maintaining this phase, from the absolute 
amounts of expenditure range from several hours to 1-2 days).
The law o f supercompensation also applies to creatine phosphate, the enzymatic and structural 
proteins, to the phosolipids, and to a number of mitochondria in the muscle fibers - in a word, for 
all products and structures, which to one or another degree, were expended or destroyed during 
the muscular activity and are resynthesized during the time of rest (Yakovlev, 144).
The phase of supercompensation appears as a first step in adaptation of the body to muscular ac­
tivity (Yakovlev, 138). Regardless of its short term (from several hours to 2-3 days), it is ensures 
execution of the following loads in conditions that are more favorable to the body.
In systematic execution of increasing loads, the after effects left by each of them are summed up, 
leading to stable adaptation of the body, a state of trainedness. A more general form of the latter 
(from a biochemical position) is characterized by an increase in the energy potential of the body 
and ability to use it in restoration. In the base of this is the increased activity of many enzymatic
523

SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
systems accommodating changes in the regulation of the metabolic processes, and likewise, 
maintaining homeostasis.
As a result, the emerging adaptational changes from the muscular activity lead to fewer distur­
bances of the ATP balance and less disturbance of homeostasis in the trained body. In execution 
of these loads, according to their intensity or duration close to the limit (which, under the influ­
ence of training constantly moves further out) the trained body can withstand disturbances of 
homeostasis more easily. All of this ensures the ability to execute work at a given intensity 
longer, that is, greater endurance.
In the end, the positive correlation between catabolic and anabolic processes, brought out by the 
loaded muscle activity, is expressed in the following.
The intensity of the biochemical restitution in the after-work period, the same as the expressed 
phases of supercompensation of the maintained sources for movement, is spread out over the 
time of muscular activity, and positively correlates with the intensity of their dispersion. The 
greater the energy expenditure and breakdown of protein structures in the process of work, then 
to the greatest extent, will be the recovery that follows.
In this way, the biochemical shifts in the muscle fibers brought out by the muscular activity, de­
termines the following phasic changes in their energy exchange and the increase in the energy 
balance in the after-work period that appears initially for activation of the adaptational biosyn­
thesis (Yakovlev, 143).
Many complex studies (see the revues of 24 and 25) have convincingly shown that the laws of 
supercompensation of products and energy applies not only in short term muscular work but also 
to conditions of prolonged training as for example, when using methodological methods of con­
centrating SPP (specialized physical preparation) loads on time limited stages (10-12 weeks).
Thus, in multiple studies directed to studying the capabilities of rationalizing the training in the 
yearly cycle, and most frequently in track and field running (Levchenko. 71, Dubinin, 51, Nar- 
skin. 87, Vrublevsky, 39) and jumping (Antonova. 1, Mironenko, 82, Nikitin, 88, Dushenkov 52. 
Umarov, 117) volleyball (Naraliev. 86), tennis (Verkhoshansky, 12), rowing (Turcheniuk. 114), 
judo (Koptev, 64), weightlifting (Ganchenko 40), and others.
It was found that there is a long decrease in the functional abilities of athletes during periods (or 
stages) of using concentrated (that is. conccntrated in a limited time period) strength loads. After 
concluding the strength loads all the functional indices not only return to the initial level but sub­
stantially go above it (Figure 7).
This phenomenon received the name of long term delayed training effect (LDTE) (Vcrkho­
shansky, 18, 23, 24, 25,280, 281. 283).
It has been established that:
1. 
Concentrated single purpose training loads are an effective way to ensure a deeper training 
effect on the athlete’s body.
2. 
The greater (within optimal limits) the decrease in the stage of concentrated loads, the 
higher the following rise in the phase of realization of the LDTE (graphs f| and f2). Ex­

===== PDF 536 / p.525 =====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
tremely concentrated loads lead to a more significant decrease in functional indices and to a 
disruption in adaptation (graph fj).
When using concentrated loads orientated to achieving the LDTE, the methods used should 
not be extremely intense. Concentration, in one of the single purpose loads, is already in­
tensification of the training effect and to increase it with highly intense means of training 
does not follow.
Realization of LDTE of concentrated loads is served by moderate increases in work volume 
and gradually increasing intensity (B).
. 
The duration of the appearance of LDTE is determined by the volume and duration of the 
concentrated loads used. In principle, the steady appearance of LDTE (t2 ) is equal to the du­
ration of the stage (ti). In real conditions of training high level athletes, the tendency has 
been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks. It follows, however, to keep in mind 
that the appearance of LDTE has an independent character and to a significant degree, de­
pends upon the ability of the athlete to withstand volume loads and the ability of his body 
for recovery. The same volume loads in two athletes having the same qualifications can 
have a different effect.
>. 
In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body rela­
tively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work 
volume. The latter is expressed by a slowdown in increases and even a decrease in the func­
tional abilities. For example. Figure 8 shows that in triple jumpers, after the concentrated 
specialized strength preparation loads in March-April, the LDTE acquired showed an in­
crease in speed-strength and increased sports results in May-June.

ete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team,

ity and an objective prerequisite in a rational system of high level athlete preparation. Purposeful

Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation 
of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide 
moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or an­
other functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reac­
tions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body.
The reason for such happenings is tied in with the changes in the external interactions of the 
body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mas­
tery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, 
and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakov­
lev, 144 ).
There are three levels of adaptation restructuring, each of which has its own specific character in 
regard to heterochronicity of the accommodating restructuring and their corresponding physio­
logical processes and structural transformation (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky, 
Viru.28, 286 ).
1.6.

They are:
level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and 
immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions); 
level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the 
structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation); 
level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation).
On the first level there are fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecu­
tiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9).
In work, there is high excitation energy necessary for the muscle work and in the post work pe­
riod. liquidation of the biochemical changes that have taken place in the muscles and other or­
gans during the time of muscular work.
The most expressed changes are observed in energy exchange. In the muscle work there is a de­
crease in the content of the substrates for energy conversion (creatine phosphate, glycogen, and 
during long term work even the lipids) and an increase in the content of intercellular metabolism 
products.
The accumulation of these products and the stronger hormonal activity stimulates the oxidative 
processes in the tissues in the rest period after work. This serves to restore the intramuscular re­
serve of energy products, which leads to normalization of the water-electrolyte balance of the 
body and ensures the inductive synthesis of proteins in the organs that were subjected to the 
loads (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38).
The process of restoration, during the period of rest after muscular work, takes place at different 
speeds and ends at different times (Table 2).

Oxygen reserves and creatine phosphate in the working muscles are the fastest to recover fol­
lowed by inter muscular reserves of glycogen and liver glycogen and then the fat reserves that 
were used up during the protein structure work.
It is known that the intensity of the flow of the restorative processes, and the periods of filling 
the energy reserves in the body, depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure dur­
ing the time of muscular work (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38).
In the formation of compensatory accustomization restructuring, a definite consecutiveness in the 
improvement of physiological factors that determine the working effect of the motor functions 
can be clearly seen (Verkhoshansky 17, 24, 281- 284).
In a loaded work regime a shift in the 
functional characteristics of the body is 
observed first (Figure 10).
Intensification of this function acti­
vates a corresponding morphological 
(structural) restructuring (2), which, 
comes out as a quality material base 
for the adaptation process. This makes 
it possible to get further intensification 
of this function. Development of these 
mutually conditioning processes in 
turn, creates the prerequisites for rais­
ing the effect (power) of the external 
work of the body, which is reached by 
the more complete realization o f the 
motor potential of the body (Verkho­
shansky, 26, 27, 283, 284).
On the global level of the functional 
systemic restructuring of the body, development of adaptational changes are realized first of all 
because of the improved strength of the bio energetic processes. Following this is the bio energy 
volume and finally, improved bioenergetic effectiveness (economy) characterized by the level of 
use of the released energy into the metabolic processes for execution of specific muscle work.
In relation to separate bio energetic systems, the consecutiveness of development of adaptation 
during training takes on the following form: a faster increase in the capability of the aerobic oxi­
dative processes and maintenance of glycogen in the working muscles. Following this is mainte­
nance of the myofibril proteins (actin and myosin) and intensity of glycolosis. At the end, after 
everything - is maintenance of creatine phosphate (CP) and activeness of the creatine phos- 
phokinasis in the muscles (Margaria et al, 242, Yakovlev, 144, Volkov 38).
In this way, we get the greatest tempo of development and a longer period of maintaining a 
maximally high level that is characteristic for the biochemical indices of endurance for long term 
work, i.e., the aerobic abilities of the athlete. There is significantly slower development and 
shorter maintenance of a maximally high level of the biochemical indices of speed-strength 
qualities and speed endurance (Volkov, 38, Yakovlev, 144).
Several aspects of the heterochronicity phenomena of adaptation restructuring will be looked at 
further on in the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization of the athlete's body.

In the process of forming the behavioral adaptation reactions during strenuous muscle activity 
with complex motor coordination, attention is first given to the economically wasteful generali­
zation phase. This is seen in an abundance of extra movements in generally constrained move­
ments, motor system errors and a sharply expressed vegetative component (Bernstein. 7). Further 
on, according to the amount of skill formation and consolidation of extra movements in the mo­
tor system errors are eliminated and the vegetative component of the reaction is significantly de­
creased. In this way the end result becomes sufficient for maximum economy of the body re­
sources (Bernstein, 7, Farfel, 120, Verkhoshansky, 17, 25, 281, 281, Person, 95, 96, Donskoy, 
50, Granit, 210).
In this way, during successful adaptation to very different factors in the environment, high func­
tional economy appears to be a general characteristic trait of the systems, responsible for the ad­
aptation. This trait appears on different level of the system activity' as follows:
- 
on both the cellular and organ levels, where it is determined by the ratio of the different cel­
lular structures involved in the adaptive response;
on the level of the systems as a whole, where it is determined by the ratio of different or­
gans; and finally
on the level of neuro-humoral regulation, where economy appears as a consequence of 
greater reactiveness of the adapted organs to the mediator and hormone actions (Meerson, 
77, Viru, Kirge, 35, Haydarliu, 124).
One of the indicators of the athlete's adaptation to physical loads appears to be economy of the 
physiological systems functioning at rest and during moderate, sub-maximal loads. At the same 
time, during maximum loads, the body is capable of achieving a level of system functioning 
which is not possible by the untrained body (Farfel, 120, Pshennikova, 99). This feature is seen 
both within the limits of compensation as well as in the results of long term adaptation (Verkho­
shansky, Viru. 28. 286).
For example, the schematic on Figure 11 shows that doing low power work is easy for both the 
trained and untrained person, as differences in the physiological shifts (changes in energy expen­
diture, minute blood volume, breathing fre­
quency, etc.) are hardly seen. In more in­
tense work, in the untrained, a more sub­
stantial physiological shift takes place than 
in the trained, and with increases in the

even

untrained, the functional shifts in them 
reach maximum, but in the trained they are 
still moderate, that is, for them this work is 
comparatively not hard.
The trained athlete can accomplish work
1.7. 
F u n ctio n al econom y o f the a d a p te d body
530

===== PDF 542 / p.531 =====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
with intensities that are significantly higher than those, wrhich for the untrained, appear to be 
maximal. In this, corresponding physiological shifts continue to increase. In the end, it reaches a 
limit work intensity and at this moment for the trained athletes it registers a maximum functional 
shift (Pshennicova, 99).
Means of economizing body functions during loaded muscle activity are extremely diverse and 
are determined by the functional specifics of the life ensuring systems of the body.
For example, in adaptation to loaded muscular activity requiring endurance, a significant in­
crease in the number of mitochondria in the skeletal muscles leads to a state that when at rest, or 
when the muscles are loaded, the portion of oxygen extracted from each liter of the flowing 
blood is greater than in the untrained body. As a result, an extreme increase in the minute volume 
of the heart during loaded activity shows up as being superfluous and ensures economy of blood 
circulation (Pshennikova, 99). Together with this, an increase in the strength of the mitochondrial 
system serves to increase the intensity of pyruvate utilization, decreasing its transition to lactate 
and consequently less accumulation of lactate in the muscles (Morgan et al., 250, Hollocszy, 
219, Riedy et al, 259).
In the end, the increased aerobic power of the body leads to an increase in its ability to utilize 
lipids to provide energy. The lipids have less of an energy effect in comparison to carbohydrates, 
but apparently they are used as a quality substrate for oxidation, sharply increasing the amount of 
energy as a consequence of their practically inexhaustible supply (Yakovlev, 140. Panin, 94, 
Haidarliu, 124) As a result, it allows for more economical use of glycogen during loaded activity 
(Holloszy et al, 224, Davies et al. 167, Galbo, 203).
The economic effect of adaptation of the body to physical loads on the level of the cardio­
vascular system has been given sufficient detailed study. The advantage of training the heart 
muscle together with changes in body adaptation, as a whole, ensures economic functioning of 
the heart at rest and during sub maximal physical loads. A decreased level of heart function at 
rest and a smaller functional increase during moderate loads, is conditioned in the trained body 
mainly by ncreased oxygen volume in the blood, increased ability of the tissues to extract oxygen 
from the blood (Yakovlev, 140, Astrand, Rodahl, 148) and greater micro circulation because of 
the widened capillary network in the skeletal muscles involved in fulfilling the main load, which 
makes it possible to increase the contact surface between the blood and muscle tissue.
Together with this, there is a decrease in the peripheral resistance of the vessels (Osoliny, 93). 
The main role in this is played by the formation of peripheral circulatory reactions that ensure 
effective redistribution of the blood flow and regulation of the oxygen entering into primarily the 
mobilized tissues and organs (Vasilieva, 11, Osoliny 93, Yankovsky, 146) and the stress on the 
anaerobic metabolites (Vasilieva, 11, Karlsson. 71, 232, Gollnik, Hermansen, 206). It is mainly 
these adaptive achievements that decrease the need for circulation and respiration in the body 
and make it possible to have normal provision of oxygen to the tissues and substrates with de­
creased minute blood volume.
The main role in the economy of functions of the trained heart, is played by the increased tension 
and speed of relaxation of the heart muscles (Meerson, Chashina, 79, Vasilieva, Stiopochkina,
10, De Maria et al., 188), and likewise the change in neuro-humoral regulation of the heart, de­
531

===== PDF 543 / p.532 =====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
veloped in the process of adaptation to the physical loads (Lin. Horvath. 237, Bolter, Gordon. 
158).
As a result of adaptation, there is an increase in the power and at the same time, economy of the 
motor system. Accommodation to the changes in the mechanisms directing muscular activity on 
the CNS level, leads to improvement of intra- and inter- muscular coordination, making it possi­
ble to mobilize a greater number of motor units during the loads and to synchronize their activity 
where strong concentrated effort is needed.
At the same time physical training leads to greater economy in the functioning of the neuromus­
cular system, and in the electrical activity of the skeletal muscles. There is an appreciable in­
crease in electrical activity in the muscles and fast development of fatigue is noticed in athletes 
during execution of the loads that are impossible for the untrained person (Yaschaninas, 147).
The main role in economy of energy in complex coordination motor actions is played by the se­
lection of the optimal, that is, more favorable movement due to the external strength and meta­
bolic energy generated by the body. Most frequently their interaction is accounted for by the 
formation of a so - called biodynamic structure, i.e., an expedient, steady means of tying together 
the accented moments of active and reactive dynamics in a movement system. With this, the lat­
ter becomes totally functionally oriented and specialized, and with this, responds to accommo­
date the external situation and the working mechanism for resolving motor tasks (Verkho­
shansky, 15, 19, 24, 25).
Finally, in a large group of sports (running, rowing, jumping, weightlifting), the active working 
effort is preceded by a sharp stretch of the muscles, whose elastic properties ensure accumulation 
of elastic (resilient) energy in the muscles. This energy provides economy to the movement sys­
tem as a whole (see reviews of the Author -18, 20).
In the process of forming steady, long term adaptation to physical loads, a restructuring takes 
place in the hormonal-humoral regulation of the functional systems involved in the adaptation 
(Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, 288, Meerson, 76, Viru, Kirge, 35, Pishniak, 100). In the adapted 
body, hormonal linked regulation functions more economically. In response to one and the same 
load in a trained body, there a significant decrease in the activation of the hormonal system to­
gether with correspondingly smaller increases in the concentration of hormones in the blood, 
than in the untrained body. This is accompanied by a limited stress reaction and absence of a 
negative, damaging component of this reaction, tied in with excessive “dispersal" of hormones

Here however, it is necessary to note that if a significant portion of time is devoted to execution

competitive exercise by gradually increasing execution almost up to maximum speed.

1.10. General schematic of the adaptational process during sports activity
The process of adaptation is determined principally by the following components:
A) 
Biosynthesis;
B) 
Internal factors;
C) 
Mechanisms of their interactions (Kaznacheev, 59).
In evaluating any of these components, it is necessary to consider the properties of a single pur­
pose biosystem (aim of system control) and conditions (situations) to overcome, which the body 
requires in adaptation.
Multiple studies have produced a store of scientific knowledge on the theory of adaptation. Ex­
amined (studied) were the essentials of adaptation of man to extreme conditions of his surround­
ings, both social and native, and frequently climatic-geographic factors, artificially changing the 
surrounding conditions, change in the geographical zone and changes in the daily dynamics of 
the functions, of one or several factors, the form of fractional, continuous and cross sectional ad­
aptation and so on.
Characteristic for all of these conditions are the specific essentials of the general laws of devel­
opment of the adaptational process and the mechanisms of their realization.
The content and structure of the general theory of adaptation is sufficiently complex (and it 
should be noted, insufficiently regulated). Because of this, in order to not remain on the ascer­
tained or declarative level; the essence of which contains unsubstantiated, non-constructive dis­
cussion and conclusions, it follows to describe completely, the specifics of the adaptational proc­
ess and the essentials for realization of the adaptational mechanism during sports activity. This 
is all the more necessary7 in order to determine the place for presenting the specific essentials of 
the adaptational process in sport, within the limits of general adaptation, and to effectively use its 
principal position in interpreting literary and original experimental data.
Based on all the material looked at above, it is possible to conclude that the process of adaptation 
during sports activity is characterized by a constant system-discreet influences of the adaptogenic 
factor on the body, ensuring progressive improvement (development) of his specific motor abili­
ties. This means that the adaptation factor function is not permanent (as let us say in adaptation

in time. Between the adaptogenic factor influences, developed by their activation, is the accom­
modative restructuring (change) in the body, of converted, discreet influences in a steady (un­
broken) flow of a continuous process that is progressively developed.
In this way, on the basis of the material looked at above, long term adaptation to sports activity 
can be presented as an uninterrupted cyclical changing event, tied in with exhaustion and restora­
tion of CAR in the body. Moving away from here, the morpho-functional acquisition carries a 
definite qualitative and quantitative change in the complex of external and internal relationships 
in the body. This ensures a higher level of specialized workability of the athlete and greater pro­
gress in his mastery'.
It is correct to propose that this process develops both vertically as well as horizontally (Verkho­
shansky, Viru, 28, 286). In other words, the accommodative restructurings have a concrete level 
of structure, functioning within the limits of definite segments (phases) of coordinated time (Fig­
ure 15).
The process of adaptation begins with activation of specific homeostatic reactions (first level of 
adaptation). Repeat shifts in constant internal surroundings in the body and strengthening the re­
serves of energy and plastic provision brings about activation of non-specific mechanisms of ad­
aptation and transition to compensatory adaptation (second level).
The mechanism of compensatory adaptation provides relatively stoic morpho-functional im­
provement in the cellular structure, which appears as an unchanging condition for development 
of long term adaptation, transforming the body into a new, higher level of specialized capabilities 
(third level).

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** the two share the idea that systems
gain and lose adaptation on different timelines, but their orderings conflict: the baseline
has aerobic lost fastest and alactic slowest, while Platonov's reverse order (stated for
overtraining, printed 86) has CP lost first and oxidative/glycogen last. Record this as a
tension, not a convergence.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
three-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist. The source states the reverse-order loss for overtraining,
not for simple layoffs; the entry's own extension to detraining/layoffs beyond what the
text states is this entry's inference, not the authors' claim.

**Example** — Inference: by the stated reverse order, CP-related qualities (gained last)
would be lost first, and oxidative and glycogen qualities lost last. The source states this
reverse order for overtraining, not for a training layoff; it separately notes that longer
training makes the accompanying biochemical changes persist longer after cessation
(printed 86), which is the closest the text comes to describing simple detraining.

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).

The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.

The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)

**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology). From 9.1: [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]] (9.1, Fig 5).

**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky's own paper uses supercompensation without the 1.16 reservation (both checked against the page images). One of the three bases of the constructive effect is "supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins)" (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519), and by the "rule of V.Engelgard," "in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)" (PDF 533 / p.522). This adds a within-book contradiction to the contest recorded above. See [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] and [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]].

# The Long-Term Delayed Training Effect: Volume Well Above the Optimum Depresses Speed-Strength, Then a Timed Volume Cut Lets It Rise Above Baseline

**What it is** — The authors report "a steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 weeks)" caused by "voluminous strength loading," after which "speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it" (Nikitin 1977; Mironenko 1979; Antonova 1982; Levchenko 1982). Because this "does not agree with established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness" and "is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining," it became "a subject of special study" (PDF p. 374 / printed p. 363, checked against the page image). They then state a dose-response rule: "The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body reacts with diminished response." "If the volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. This intense rise in special work-capacity is the phenomenon known as the long-term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (same page).

Their characterisation (Fig 6.31, PDF pp. 374-375 / printed pp. 363-364, checked against the page images), points 1, 2 and 4:
1. "Concentration of strength loading is the basic condition for the beginning of the LDTE."
2. "The lower the speed-strength levels fall (within an optimal range) during the concentration of strength loading stage, the higher they rise in the subsequent LDTE phase (graphs of F1 and F2). Excessive concentration of strength loading leads to a more significant drop in speed-strength and disruption of adaptation (graph F3)." In the figure, F3 dips lowest and only creeps back toward the baseline by the end of T2; F1 and F2 end above it.
4. "A subsequent moderate volume of general developmental work, combined with special work of gradually increasing intensity contributes to eliciting the LDTE."

Points 3 (non-intensive means) and 5 (T2 about equal to T1, observed 4-12 weeks, individualised) are already quoted in [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] and [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]].

**Figures.** Fig 6.29 (sprinters, PDF p. 374, read from the image): a shaded rectangle marks the loading period from month 0 to about month 2.5; three curves (starting, explosive and absolute strength, the dips not labelled separately) fall to about 85-96% of initial, recross 100% at about month 2, and at month 4 sit at about 125% (starting), about 119% (explosive) and about 112% (absolute). Fig 6.30 (middle-distance runners, Zhdanovich 1980, PDF p. 375): during a shaded block from about month 1.6 to about month 4.5 (read from a 300 dpi render of the page image), vertical jump rises to about 7% and then falls to about 4.5% by month 8; stride length and ten standing long jumps keep rising after the block, to about 11% and about 9-9.5%. The text says vertical jump falls in the competition stage and offers a hedged reason: "One may assume that the reason for this phenomenon is the increase in volume of intense distance work" (PDF p. 374). LDTE after concentrated strength loading is also reported in swimming (Rudokene 1981) and ice-skating (Kabachkova et al 1982).

Two further points: athletes "invariably do not allow or do not have sufficient time for recuperation after extensive strength loading," which minimises the LDTE and forces the body "to unjustifiably deplete its current adaptation energy and sometimes draw upon its deep adaptation energy" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). And "one must differentiate between maintenance of the training effect and the LDTE of loading": maintenance is "the retention of functional adaptation for a given period after training has ceased"; the LDTE is "the relatively prolonged increase in the functional indicators as a result of specially organised, concentrated volumes of loading" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors say the volume-performance link is "characteristically simple" but give no physiological mechanism for the delayed rise in 6.10's strength material; they note that the "physiological conditions, mechanisms and characteristics of the LDTE until recently have not been a subject of much research" (PDF p. 374). Inference: the library holds two readings of the same curve shape, supercompensation or adaptive reconstruction ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]) and fitness-fatigue, where fatigue masks fitness until volume drops ([[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]); the book does not settle between them here.

**When to apply** — Planning a concentrated strength block for an advanced athlete when the aim is a later rise in speed-strength, accepting a planned dip during the block. Inference: a dip in speed-strength during such a block is the expected path, not by itself a signal to stop. Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: the LDTE rests on one load-design move, the timed volume cut, so it fits that practice. Eric's baseline: "The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds" (line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: during a deliberate block, an mRSI drop below an athlete's usual band would be expected; the authors' own rule separates a dip "within an optimal range" from the F3 case, but gives no threshold for telling them apart.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no numbers for "optimum," "within an optimal range" or "excessive," and says the effect is individual (PDF p. 375). Figs 6.29-6.31 carry no sample sizes or statistics; Fig 6.31 is a "general scheme," not data. The 5-12 weeks on PDF p. 374 is the length of the loading stages; the 4-12 weeks on PDF p. 375 is how long the LDTE lasts. They are different quantities. The book uses 4-12 weeks for three things: how long unidirectional training stays effective (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image), how long the LDTE lasts (PDF p. 375), and, in Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, translated by Yessis; PDF p. 515), the length of the concentrated stages themselves: "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image). Both PDF p. 375 and the Addendum (PDF p. 536) say the LDTE lasts about as long as the loading stage (T2 about equal to T1). Inference: this reconciles those two readings, and the PDF p. 305 figure is a separate quantity. Keep the locator with the number. Inference: in-season, when performance is needed every week, a planned multi-week dip conflicts with Eric's baseline that "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)); this is an off-season tool. The book's claim that the dip comes without "marked signs of overtraining" sits beside Bompa's framing of concentrated loading as planned overreaching ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]); Inference: that is a difference of labels, not of the observed curve.

**Example** — The authors' own: in sprinters (Fig 6.29), about 2.5 months of concentrated strength loading drove starting, explosive and absolute strength to about 85-96% of initial; by month 4 they stood at about 112-125% (values read from the image, PDF p. 374).

From 9.1: [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1, LDTE as the long level of the constructive effect), [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]] (9.1, strategy C).

**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky's own paper places the LDTE as the second of "two levels of the constructive effect" (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)." The first level is session supercompensation. See [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]].

# Put Technical Training in the Delayed-Effect Window, and Keep Competition-Period Strength Work Short, Intense and Small

**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).

The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).

**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors give no day-level timing.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, "Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis"; PDF p. 515 / printed p. 504, checked against the page image) restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: an "insignificant increase" in specialised strength volume "(by only a few percent)" to "maintain" the achieved level "led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, checked against the page image). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip: its own example fits Chapter 6, and the Addendum is a separate translation of Verkhoshansky's text, which makes a translation slip plausible. The book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376), so the separation is a matter of emphasis.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own, from the Addendum (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image): the text says its Figure 8 shows that "in triple jumpers," concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April were followed by a rise in speed-strength and results in May-June; raising strength volume "by only a few percent" to hold the gain then brought "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results." The page switches from plural to singular here: the volume rise was "as believed by the athlete," and "the athlete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team." Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]] (6.12.2, the same strength-then-technique question from a later passage); [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]] (6.12.2, the reduced-loading stage after large volumes must last far longer than the usual 1-2 week unload; its "no more volume" instruction is rule 2 here)

15	# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops
16	
17	**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
18	training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
19	oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
20	protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
21	only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
22	these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
23	training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
24	those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
25	This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
26	tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
27	a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
28	glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
29	disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)
30	
31	**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
32	structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
33	mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
34	then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
35	others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
36	this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

101	88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
102	biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)
103	
104	**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
105	substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
106	stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
107	overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
108	precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
109	heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.
110	
111	**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
112	[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
113	"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
114	literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
115	model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
116	for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
117	glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
118	include; use both together rather than duplicating either.
119	
120	**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of

124	techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
125	periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
126	supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
127	on periodization design.
128	
129	**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
130	application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
131	for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
132	by the same evidence.
133	
134	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
