# Verkhoshansky Extends the Supercompensation Law From the Session to Concentrated Training Stages of 10-12 Weeks

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 535 / p.524, checked against the page image): "Many complex studies (see the revues of 24 and 25) have convincingly shown that the laws of supercompensation of products and energy applies not only in short term muscular work but also to conditions of prolonged training as for example, when using methodological methods of concentrating SPP (specialized physical preparation) loads on time limited stages (10-12 weeks)." The studies were "directed to studying the capabilities of rationalizing the training in the yearly cycle," in "track and field running (Levchenko. 71, Dubinin, 51, Narskin. 87, Vrublevsky, 39) and jumping (Antonova. 1, Mironenko, 82, Nikitin, 88, Dushenkov 52. Umarov, 117) volleyball (Naraliev. 86), tennis (Verkhoshansky, 12), rowing (Turcheniuk. 114), judo (Koptev, 64), weightlifting (Ganchenko 40), and others." The finding: "there is a long decrease in the functional abilities of athletes during periods (or stages) of using concentrated (that is. concentrated in a limited time period) strength loads. After concluding the strength loads all the functional indices not only return to the initial level but substantially go above it (Figure 7). This phenomenon received the name of long term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (PDF 535 / p.524).

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's framing: the LDTE is the same law as the session overshoot ([[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]]), acting over weeks. Inference: this sentence states the link between the two levels that [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] records as unstated on PDF 530; it is still an assertion, since no mechanism for the long level is given here.

**When to apply** — When placing a concentrated strength or SPP block in the year and explaining to staff why the athlete will be flat during it. The list of sports gives the range the author claims: running, jumping, volleyball, tennis, rowing, judo, weightlifting.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own sport list for the finding, from running and jumping to weightlifting and judo (PDF 535 / p.524). # One Triple Jumper's Year (Fig 8): Two Concentrated Strength-and-Bounding Blocks, Each Followed by a Rise in Strength and Jump Results

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky gives Fig 8 as his example of the LDTE (9.1 §1.5, PDF 536 / p.525 text, PDF 537 / p.526 figure; figure read from a 300 dpi render of the page image). The caption: "Dynamics of the speed-strength parameters, the volumes of the carried out training loads and the sport results of the triple jumper during the yearly cycle (from October - to August)." Top panel: monthly "P0, maximal strength," "Fmax, magnitude of the maximal explosive effort," and "Jd., index of explosive strength," on a left axis in "Kg" (160 to 200) and a right axis in "Kg/sec" (350 to 550); the figure does not say which line uses which axis. Middle panel: triple-jump result in m. Bottom panel: monthly "barbell exercises (in tones - on the left axe)," "bounds" in km on the right axis, and "the whole competition exercises executions (number of repetitions - on the left axe)." Approximate readings from the image (months X to VIII):
- Barbell, tonnes: 35, 75, 16, 14, 1, 75, 58, 19, 4, 16, 2.
- Bounds, km: 7.3, 9.3, 1.8, 0.4, 1.0, 8.6, 5.0, 0.5, 0.6, 1.0, 0.6.
- Triple jumps, repetitions: 20, 34, 73, 44, 20, 36, 95, 60, 40, 50, 30.
- P0, kg: 170, 172, 178, 192, 190, 183, 192, 194, 200, 196, 200.
- Fmax and Jd, read on the left scale: Fmax about 166 to 188, dipping in III and VII; Jd about 165, 161, 168, 173, 175, 164, 160, 172, 174, 169, 177, its low point in IV.
- Triple jump, m (plotted from XII): 15.96, 16.22, 16.06, 16.04, 16.02, 16.46, 16.30, 15.98, 16.50.

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's reading (PDF 536 / p.525): "after the concentrated specialized strength preparation loads in March-April, the LDTE acquired showed an increase in speed-strength and increased sports results in May-June. [H]owever, an insignificant increase in their volume in specialized strength preparation (by only a [f]ew percent) in order to 'maintain' the achieved level of specialized workability (as believed by [t]he athlete) led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results. As a result of this, the ath[l]ete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team." This quote is partly reconstructed: the left margin of the page is clipped in the scan, so the bracketed letters are missing on the page image. He uses it to illustrate his point 6: in the LDTE period "volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily ... but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (same page).

**When to apply** — As a worked picture of what the dip and rebound look like in one athlete's monthly numbers, when planning where a concentrated strength block ends relative to the main competitions. Inference: the figure shows the pattern twice, not once. A first block in X-XI (barbell 75 t and bounds 9.3 km in XI) is followed by P0 and the jump rising to a winter peak in I (192 kg, 16.22 m); the second block in III-IV (75 t and 8.6 km in III) is followed by the May-June peak the text names. The text mentions only March-April.

**When NOT to apply** — One athlete, readings by eye, and no statistics, so `supported` here means a described case with printed data, not a tested rule. Three mismatches between text and figure: the text says "in triple jumpers" (plural) while the caption and the rest of the passage are singular; the text says the strength volume rose "by only a few percent," but the figure's barbell volume goes from about 4 t in VI to about 16 t in VII and bounds from about 0.6 to 1.0 km (Inference: that is a large relative rise from a small base, so the "few percent" may mean a share of total volume; the page does not say); and the August rebound to about 16.50 m, the best mark in the figure, is not discussed. Jump repetitions also rose from VI to VII (about 40 to 50), so the July drop cannot be laid on strength volume alone (Inference). Point 6 itself reads the other way round from Chapter 6, which is recorded as a contest in [[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]].

**Example** — From the figure: in III the barbell volume is about 75 t and bounds about 8.6 km, Jd falls to its low in IV, and in V the jump rises from about 16.02 m to about 16.46 m with barbell volume cut to about 19 t (PDF 537 / p.526, approximate image readings).

**Related** — [[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]] (6.10, which quotes the same text), [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[claim--supercompensation-laws-extend-to-concentrated-spp-stages-of-10-12-weeks]], [[case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]] (two concentrated strength blocks a year)

# Adaptation Is Heterochronic and Runs on Three Levels: Quick Homeostatic Reactions, Compensatory Structural Change, Long-Term Systemic Restructuring

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.6, "Heterochronism of the adaptational restructuring" (PDF 538 / p.527, checked against the page image). Verkhoshansky: "Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or another functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reactions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body." The three levels, each with "its own specific character in regard to heterochronicity" (PDF 538-539 / pp.527-528):
1. "level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions)";
2. "level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation)";
3. "level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation)."
The first level is detailed by Fig 9 and Table 2 ([[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]); the second and third by Fig 10 ([[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]]).

**Why it works** — The stated causes of heterochronicity: "the changes in the external interactions of the body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mastery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakovlev, 144)" (PDF 538 / p.527).

**When to apply** — When reading a monitoring trend: a fast marker (a session's metabolic response) and a slow one (structural or whole-system change) are expected to move at different times, so a lack of change in a slow marker after a few weeks is not by itself a failed block. Inference: the three levels map onto session, block and multi-year time scales; the page names the levels but gives no durations for them.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a conceptual scheme with citations (Verkhoshansky 24, 25; Verkhoshansky and Viru 28, 286) and no data. The same three levels reappear as the opening of 1.10 on PDF 554 (outside this batch); 9a's Viru scheme ([[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]]) is a related but separate sequence (specific, general, long-term). The page says more on heterochronicity is in "the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization" (PDF 540 / p.529), which is outside this batch.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own level 1: "fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecutiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9)" (PDF 539 / p.528).

**Related** — [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]] (1.16), [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]], [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]], [[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]], [[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]]

# The Work-Recovery Chain (Fig 9): ATP Breakdown and Metabolites in Work, Then Oxidation, ATP Production, CP and Glycogen Supercompensation, and Protein Synthesis in Recovery

**What it is** — Fig 9, "The sequence of the reparative biosynthesises in the muscles during the work and recovery (N. Yakovlev, 1986)" (9.1 §1.6, PDF 538 / p.527, read from the page image). A double horizontal line splits "Work" (below) from "Recovery" (above). Work, from the bottom: "Muscular activity" leads to "Demolition of ATP," then "Changing in the ATP balance," then "Accumulation of metabolites." Two side paths feed in: "Consumption of glycogen and fat acids" leads to "Partial ATP re-synthesis," which feeds the ATP-balance box; and "Muscular activity" leads to "Oxygen deficit (working hypoxia)," which feeds "Accumulation of metabolites." Recovery, from the line upward: "Oxygenation of metabolites," "Increase in the ATP production," "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents," "Synthesis of proteins." A side arrow also runs from "Increase in the ATP production" straight to "Synthesis of proteins." The text (PDF 539 / p.528, checked against the page image): in work, substrates fall ("creatine phosphate, glycogen, and during long term work even the lipids") and metabolism products rise; "The accumulation of these products and the stronger hormonal activity stimulates the oxidative processes in the tissues in the rest period after work. This serves to restore the intramuscular reserve of energy products, which leads to normalization of the water-electrolyte balance of the body and ensures the inductive synthesis of proteins in the organs that were subjected to the loads (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38)."

**Why it works** — In the scheme, the metabolites made in work are the trigger for the recovery chain: they drive oxidation, which powers the restoration of energy stores and then protein synthesis. Inference: this is the same metabolite-as-inducer idea 9a recorded ([[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]), drawn as a sequence.

**When to apply** — As the first-level picture in [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], when explaining why protein synthesis comes last in recovery, after energy stores. Inference: it supports the 9a caution that clearing metabolites during rest may blunt the later steps ([[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a flow chart credited to Yakovlev (1986) with no data or timings; the times are in Table 2 ([[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]). The box "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents" asserts CP supercompensation, which the 1.16 text does not accept ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]).

**Example** — The figure's recovery column in order: oxygenation of metabolites, increased ATP production, supercompensation of CP and glycogen, synthesis of proteins (PDF 538 / p.527).

**Related** — [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]

# The Work-Recovery Chain (Fig 9): ATP Breakdown and Metabolites in Work, Then Oxidation, ATP Production, CP and Glycogen Supercompensation, and Protein Synthesis in Recovery

**What it is** — Fig 9, "The sequence of the reparative biosynthesises in the muscles during the work and recovery (N. Yakovlev, 1986)" (9.1 §1.6, PDF 538 / p.527, read from the page image). A double horizontal line splits "Work" (below) from "Recovery" (above). Work, from the bottom: "Muscular activity" leads to "Demolition of ATP," then "Changing in the ATP balance," then "Accumulation of metabolites." Two side paths feed in: "Consumption of glycogen and fat acids" leads to "Partial ATP re-synthesis," which feeds the ATP-balance box; and "Muscular activity" leads to "Oxygen deficit (working hypoxia)," which feeds "Accumulation of metabolites." Recovery, from the line upward: "Oxygenation of metabolites," "Increase in the ATP production," "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents," "Synthesis of proteins." A side arrow also runs from "Increase in the ATP production" straight to "Synthesis of proteins." The text (PDF 539 / p.528, checked against the page image): in work, substrates fall ("creatine phosphate, glycogen, and during long term work even the lipids") and metabolism products rise; "The accumulation of these products and the stronger hormonal activity stimulates the oxidative processes in the tissues in the rest period after work. This serves to restore the intramuscular reserve of energy products, which leads to normalization of the water-electrolyte balance of the body and ensures the inductive synthesis of proteins in the organs that were subjected to the loads (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38)."

**Why it works** — In the scheme, the metabolites made in work are the trigger for the recovery chain: they drive oxidation, which powers the restoration of energy stores and then protein synthesis. Inference: this is the same metabolite-as-inducer idea 9a recorded ([[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]), drawn as a sequence.

**When to apply** — As the first-level picture in [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], when explaining why protein synthesis comes last in recovery, after energy stores. Inference: it supports the 9a caution that clearing metabolites during rest may blunt the later steps ([[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a flow chart credited to Yakovlev (1986) with no data or timings; the times are in Table 2 ([[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]). The box "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents" asserts CP supercompensation, which the 1.16 text does not accept ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]).

**Example** — The figure's recovery column in order: oxygenation of metabolites, increased ATP production, supercompensation of CP and glycogen, synthesis of proteins (PDF 538 / p.527).

# Restoration Times After Loaded Work, Process by Process (Table 2, Volkov 1986 and Fox 1981): Minutes for Phosphagens, Hours for Lactate and Glycogen, Up to 72 Hours for Protein Synthesis

**What it is** — "The process of restoration, during the period of rest after muscular work, takes place at different speeds and ends at different times (Table 2)" (9.1 §1.6, PDF 539 / p.528). Table 2, "Time necessary for restoration of different biochemical processes in the period of rest after loaded muscle work (According to N. Volkov, 1986 and E. Fox, 1981)," as printed (checked against the page image), in the printed order:
- "Restoration of the phosphogens in the muscles (ATP and CP)": from 2-3 min.
- "Restoration of oxygen reserves in the body": from 10-15 sec.
- "Payback/recovery of alactic oxygen debt": from 3-5 min.
- "Clearance of lactic acid": active rest from 30 min to 1 hour; passive rest from 1-2 hr.
- "Restoration of inter muscular reserves of glycogen": after long term work from 10-46 hours; after non long term work from 5-24 hours.
- "Restoration of glycogen reserves in the liver": from 12-48 hours.
- "Strengthening of inductive synthesis of enzyme and structural proteins": from 12-72 hours.

**Why it works** — The text's ordering (PDF 540 / p.529): "Oxygen reserves and creatine phosphate in the working muscles are the fastest to recover followed by inter muscular reserves of glycogen and liver glycogen and then the fat reserves that were used up during the protein structure work." The time depends on the dose: restoration "depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure during the time of muscular work" (same page). Inference: "inter muscular" is almost certainly intramuscular (the PDF 539 text says "intramuscular reserve"), and the fat-reserves clause is garbled in translation.

**When to apply** — As a rough clock for spacing work of different kinds: repeat-effort rest for phosphagens in minutes, lactate clearance helped by active rest, and 1-3 days for glycogen and the protein-synthesis response. Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: a table of this kind is a load-design tool that fits that practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a compiled summary from Volkov and a textbook (Fox), with no loads, populations or methods; the ranges are wide (glycogen after long work 10-46 hours). The table lists oxygen reserves (10-15 sec) after phosphagens (2-3 min) though it is the faster process; quote the printed order. The text's order puts fat reserves last, while the table's last and longest row is protein synthesis; fats are not in the table. The 12-72 hour protein-synthesis row should be read with Fig 5 in 9a, whose curves stay above baseline far longer ([[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]).

**Example** — From the table: lactic acid clears in 30 min to 1 hour in active rest but 1-2 hr in passive rest (PDF 539 / p.528).

**Related** — [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], [[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[heuristic--start-the-next-session-as-the-previous-sessions-protein-synthesis-ends]], [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[framework--positive-and-negative-sequences-of-endurance-loading]], [[claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]]

# Function Changes First, Structure Follows, and Work Effectiveness Rises Last but Furthest (Fig 10); Bioenergetic Power Comes Before Capacity, and Economy Comes Last

**What it is** — For the second level of adaptation (compensatory restructuring) Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.6, PDF 540 / p.529, checked against the page image): "In a loaded work regime a shift in the functional characteristics of the body is observed first (Figure 10). Intensification of this function activates a corresponding morphological (structural) restructuring (2), which, comes out as a quality material base for the adaptation process. This makes it possible to get further intensification of this function. Development of these mutually conditioning processes in turn, creates the prerequisites for raising the effect (power) of the external work of the body, which is reached by the more complete realization of the motor potential of the body (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27, 283, 284)." Fig 10 ("The rate of the dynamics of improvement of the factors which determine the working effect of the sport actions: 1. Functional characteristics 2. Morphological reconstructions 3. Effectiveness of the muscular work") draws three curves from one origin against time with no scale: curve 1 rises steeply and flattens; curve 2 rises more slowly and flattens lower; curve 3 starts slowest, nearly straight, crosses 2 and then 1, and ends highest. For the third level (global restructuring): "development of adaptational changes are realized first of all because of the improved strength of the bio energetic processes. Following this is the bio energy volume and finally, improved bioenergetic effectiveness (economy) characterized by the level of use of the released energy into the metabolic processes for execution of specific muscle work" (same page).

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's mechanism is a loop: function drives structure, and structure allows more function; the external work effect rises only as both develop (PDF 540). No data are given.

**When to apply** — When a block shows early gains that then slow while performance keeps climbing: Fig 10 says the early gains are functional, and the later performance rise is the effectiveness curve catching up. Inference: in programming terms, the first weeks of a new stimulus reward functional (largely neural and metabolic) change, and the slower structural change is what lets the effect keep growing.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Fig 10 is a schematic without axes or data, and the order of power, volume and economy is stated without a study. "Strength of the bio energetic processes" is a translation; Inference: it most likely means power (rate), as against "volume" (capacity) and "effectiveness" (efficiency).

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's Fig 10: "Effectiveness of the muscular work" starts below both other curves and ends above both (PDF 540 / p.529).

**Related** — [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear]], [[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]]

# A New Complex Skill Starts in a Wasteful Generalisation Phase; Practice Strips the Extra Movement and the Autonomic Overreaction Until It Is Economical

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.7, "Functional economy of the adapted body," opens (PDF 541 / p.530, checked against the page image): "In the process of forming the behavioral adaptation reactions during strenuous muscle activity with complex motor coordination, attention is first given to the economically wasteful generalization phase. This is seen in an abundance of extra movements in generally constrained movements, motor system errors and a sharply expressed vegetative component (Bernstein. 7). Further on, according to the amount of skill formation and consolidation of extra movements in the motor system errors are eliminated and the vegetative component of the reaction is significantly decreased. In this way the end result becomes sufficient for maximum economy of the body resources (Bernstein, 7, Farfel, 120, Verkhoshansky, 17, 25, 281, 281, Person, 95, 96, Donskoy, 50, Granit, 210)."

**Why it works** — The page names three costs of the early phase: extra movements, errors, and a "sharply expressed vegetative component" (Inference: an exaggerated autonomic response, heart rate and breathing, to the task). Skill formation removes them, which is where the economy comes from (PDF 541).

**When to apply** — When a new drill or lift is introduced and its energy cost looks out of proportion to its load. Eric's baseline: "New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 171, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the page agrees on direction but gives no time course, so the 3-4 week figure is the baseline's, not Verkhoshansky's.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: the paragraph is a summary of Bernstein and others, with no study described. "Consolidation of extra movements" reads oddly; Inference: the sense is that extra movements are removed as the skill consolidates. The passage is about "strenuous muscle activity with complex motor coordination"; it says nothing about simple or already-learned movements.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's three signs of the wasteful phase: "an abundance of extra movements in generally constrained movements, motor system errors and a sharply expressed vegetative component" (PDF 541 / p.530).

**Related** — [[claim--exercise-economy-improves-with-skill-and-interval-style-costs-more]], [[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]], [[framework--mechanisms-of-functional-economy-in-the-trained-body]], [[heuristic--progress-skills-only-at-70-80-percent-technical-reliability]]

# Adaptation Shows as Economy: Smaller Physiological Shifts at Submaximal Loads and a Higher Ceiling at Maximal Loads (Farfel, Fig 11), at Three Levels

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.7, PDF 541 / p.530, checked against the page image): "during successful adaptation to very different factors in the environment, high functional economy appears to be a general characteristic trait of the systems, responsible for the adaptation." It appears at three levels: "on both the cellular and organ levels, where it is determined by the ratio of the different cellular structures involved in the adaptive response; on the level of the systems as a whole, where it is determined by the ratio of different organs; and finally on the level of neuro-humoral regulation, where economy appears as a consequence of greater reactiveness of the adapted organs to the mediator and hormone actions (Meerson, 77, Viru, Kirge, 35, Haydarliu, 124)." The two-sided marker: "One of the indicators of the athlete's adaptation to physical loads appears to be economy of the physiological systems functioning at rest and during moderate, sub-maximal loads. At the same time, during maximum loads, the body is capable of achieving a level of system functioning which is not possible by the untrained body (Farfel, 120, Pshennikova, 99)." Fig 11 ("The principal dependence of the physiological changes (f) from the power of the executed work (N) in the trained (1) and no trained (2) athletes (V.S.Farfel, 1960)") draws two curves from the same flat start: curve 2 (untrained) turns up early and steeply; curve 1 (trained) stays flat longer and ends higher on the right. The text: low-power work is easy for both; in harder work the untrained shift more, "and with increases in the loads these differences become even greater"; at work "maximal for the untrained" their shifts are maximal while the trained are "still moderate"; and the trained can go on to "intensities that are significantly higher," reaching their own maximum shift only at their limit (Pshennicova, 99) (PDF 541-542 / pp.530-531).

**Why it works** — The page attributes the economy to the ratios of structures and organs taking part and to greater sensitivity of adapted organs to transmitters and hormones (PDF 541). The specific mechanisms are listed later in 1.7 ([[framework--mechanisms-of-functional-economy-in-the-trained-body]], [[claim--trained-body-answers-the-same-load-with-a-smaller-hormonal-response]]).

**When to apply** — When choosing a marker of adaptation: a fixed submaximal test (heart rate, lactate, perceived effort at a set load) should show a smaller shift as the athlete adapts, while a maximal test should show a higher ceiling. Inference: both are needed, because the two halves of Fig 11 move in opposite directions (less response at a fixed load, more response possible at the top).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Fig 11 is a "principal" (schematic) curve credited to Farfel (1960), with no data. The caption names the x-axis as "the power of the executed work (N)," but the drawn axis is labelled "t"; read it as work power. The page says the feature holds "both within the limits of compensation as well as in the results of long term adaptation (Verkhoshansky, Viru. 28. 286)" (PDF 541) without showing either.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: work "maximal for the untrained" brings their functional shifts to maximum, but for the trained "they are still moderate, that is, for them this work is comparatively not hard" (PDF 541 / p.530).

**Related** — [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[framework--mechanisms-of-functional-economy-in-the-trained-body]], [[claim--trained-body-answers-the-same-load-with-a-smaller-hormonal-response]], [[claim--skill-learning-moves-from-wasteful-generalisation-to-economy-bernstein]], [[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]], [[heuristic--heart-rate-work-capacity-tests-for-lifters]]

# Where the Trained Body's Economy Comes From: Muscle Oxygen Extraction and Fat Use, Peripheral Circulation and the Heart, Motor-Unit Control, Biodynamic Structure and Elastic Energy

**What it is** — "Means of economizing body functions during loaded muscle activity are extremely diverse and are determined by the functional specifics of the life ensuring systems of the body" (9.1 §1.7, PDF 542 / p.531, checked against the page images of PDF 542-543). Verkhoshansky's list, in his order:
1. **Muscle mitochondria and oxygen extraction.** In endurance adaptation "a significant increase in the number of mitochondria in the skeletal muscles" means more oxygen is "extracted from each liter of the flowing blood," so "an extreme increase in the minute volume of the heart during loaded activity shows up as being superfluous" (Pshennikova, 99). A stronger mitochondrial system raises pyruvate use, "decreasing its transition to lactate and consequently less accumulation of lactate" (Morgan et al., 250; Hollocszy, 219; Riedy et al, 259) (PDF 542).
2. **Fat use.** Higher aerobic power raises the ability "to utilize lipids," which "allows for more economical use of glycogen during loaded activity" (Holloszy et al, 224; Davies et al. 167; Galbo, 203) (PDF 542).
3. **Heart and circulation.** Lower heart function at rest and a smaller rise at moderate loads come "mainly by [i]ncreased oxygen volume in the blood, increased ability of the tissues to extract oxygen from the blood ... and greater micro circulation because of the widened capillary network"; also lower "peripheral resistance of the vessels" through "peripheral circulatory reactions that ensure effective redistribution of the blood flow." "The main role in the economy of functions of the trained heart, is played by the increased tension and speed of relaxation of the heart muscles" and by changed neuro-humoral regulation (PDF 542-543 / pp.531-532).
4. **Neuromuscular.** Better "intra- and inter- muscular coordination, making it possible to mobilize a greater number of motor units during the loads and to synchronize their activity where strong concentrated effort is needed," with "greater economy in the functioning of the neuromuscular system, and in the electrical activity of the skeletal muscles" (PDF 543 / p.532).
5. **Biodynamic structure.** "The main role in economy of energy in complex coordination motor actions is played by the selection of the optimal ... movement," usually through "a so - called biodynamic structure, i.e., an expedient, steady means of tying together the accented moments of active and reactive dynamics in a movement system" (Verkhoshansky, 15, 19, 24, 25) (PDF 543).
6. **Elastic energy.** "in a large group of sports (running, rowing, jumping, weightlifting), the active working effort is preceded by a sharp stretch of the muscles, whose elastic properties ensure accumulation of elastic (resilient) energy in the muscles. This energy provides economy to the movement system as a whole (see reviews of the Author -18, 20)" (PDF 543).
The seventh, hormonal economy, is a separate entry: [[claim--trained-body-answers-the-same-load-with-a-smaller-hormonal-response]].

**Why it works** — Each item is a way to do the same work with less central cost: more extraction per litre of blood, less glycogen per unit of work, less cardiac output, fewer wasted motor units, a better-timed movement, stored elastic energy (PDF 542-543).

**When to apply** — As a checklist of what a conditioning or technical programme can make more economical, and of the markers that should fall at a fixed submaximal load. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: items 1-3 are the routes by which that aerobic base would speed between-effort recovery; the page discusses them for endurance work, not repeat-sprint sports.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a literature list with names and numbers only, no study described. One sentence on PDF 543 reads against its own heading: "There is an appreciable increase in electrical activity in the muscles and fast development of fatigue is noticed in athletes during execution of the loads that are impossible for the untrained person (Yaschaninas, 147)." Inference: it probably refers to maximal loads, where the trained can reach a higher activity, as in Fig 11; the translation does not make that clear. "the stress on the anaerobic metabolites" (PDF 542) is unclear in translation. The square-bracketed letter in item 3 restores an "i" missing in the print ("ncreased").

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's endurance example: more mitochondria raise oxygen extraction per litre of blood, so a very large rise in cardiac output "shows up as being superfluous and ensures economy of blood circulation" (Pshennikova, 99; PDF 542 / p.531).

**What it is** — "Means of economizing body functions during loaded muscle activity are extremely diverse and are determined by the functional specifics of the life ensuring systems of the body" (9.1 §1.7, PDF 542 / p.531, checked against the page images of PDF 542-543). Verkhoshansky's list, in his order:
1. **Muscle mitochondria and oxygen extraction.** In endurance adaptation "a significant increase in the number of mitochondria in the skeletal muscles" means more oxygen is "extracted from each liter of the flowing blood," so "an extreme increase in the minute volume of the heart during loaded activity shows up as being superfluous" (Pshennikova, 99). A stronger mitochondrial system raises pyruvate use, "decreasing its transition to lactate and consequently less accumulation of lactate" (Morgan et al., 250; Hollocszy, 219; Riedy et al, 259) (PDF 542).
2. **Fat use.** Higher aerobic power raises the ability "to utilize lipids," which "allows for more economical use of glycogen during loaded activity" (Holloszy et al, 224; Davies et al. 167; Galbo, 203) (PDF 542).
3. **Heart and circulation.** Lower heart function at rest and a smaller rise at moderate loads come "mainly by [i]ncreased oxygen volume in the blood, increased ability of the tissues to extract oxygen from the blood ... and greater micro circulation because of the widened capillary network"; also lower "peripheral resistance of the vessels" through "peripheral circulatory reactions that ensure effective redistribution of the blood flow." "The main role in the economy of functions of the trained heart, is played by the increased tension and speed of relaxation of the heart muscles" and by changed neuro-humoral regulation (PDF 542-543 / pp.531-532).
4. **Neuromuscular.** Better "intra- and inter- muscular coordination, making it possible to mobilize a greater number of motor units during the loads and to synchronize their activity where strong concentrated effort is needed," with "greater economy in the functioning of the neuromuscular system, and in the electrical activity of the skeletal muscles" (PDF 543 / p.532).
5. **Biodynamic structure.** "The main role in economy of energy in complex coordination motor actions is played by the selection of the optimal ... movement," usually through "a so - called biodynamic structure, i.e., an expedient, steady means of tying together the accented moments of active and reactive dynamics in a movement system" (Verkhoshansky, 15, 19, 24, 25) (PDF 543).
6. **Elastic energy.** "in a large group of sports (running, rowing, jumping, weightlifting), the active working effort is preceded by a sharp stretch of the muscles, whose elastic properties ensure accumulation of elastic (resilient) energy in the muscles. This energy provides economy to the movement system as a whole (see reviews of the Author -18, 20)" (PDF 543).
The seventh, hormonal economy, is a separate entry: [[claim--trained-body-answers-the-same-load-with-a-smaller-hormonal-response]].

**Why it works** — Each item is a way to do the same work with less central cost: more extraction per litre of blood, less glycogen per unit of work, less cardiac output, fewer wasted motor units, a better-timed movement, stored elastic energy (PDF 542-543).

**When to apply** — As a checklist of what a conditioning or technical programme can make more economical, and of the markers that should fall at a fixed submaximal load. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: items 1-3 are the routes by which that aerobic base would speed between-effort recovery; the page discusses them for endurance work, not repeat-sprint sports.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a literature list with names and numbers only, no study described. One sentence on PDF 543 reads against its own heading: "There is an appreciable increase in electrical activity in the muscles and fast development of fatigue is noticed in athletes during execution of the loads that are impossible for the untrained person (Yaschaninas, 147)." Inference: it probably refers to maximal loads, where the trained can reach a higher activity, as in Fig 11; the translation does not make that clear. "the stress on the anaerobic metabolites" (PDF 542) is unclear in translation. The square-bracketed letter in item 3 restores an "i" missing in the print ("ncreased").

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's endurance example: more mitochondria raise oxygen extraction per litre of blood, so a very large rise in cardiac output "shows up as being superfluous and ensures economy of blood circulation" (Pshennikova, 99; PDF 542 / p.531).

# The Trained Body Answers the Same Load With a Smaller Hormonal Response, and Tissue Sensitivity to Adrenaline Falls as Trainedness Rises

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.7, PDF 543 / p.532, checked against the page image): "In the process of forming steady, long term adaptation to physical loads, a restructuring takes place in the hormonal-humoral regulation of the functional systems involved in the adaptation (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, 288, Meerson, 76, Viru, Kirge, 35, Pishniak, 100). In the adapted body, hormonal linked regulation functions more economically. In response to one and the same load in a trained body, there a significant decrease in the activation of the hormonal system together with correspondingly smaller increases in the concentration of hormones in the blood, than in the untrained body. This is accompanied by a limited stress reaction and absence of a negative, damaging component of this reaction, tied in with excessive 'dispersal' of hormones (Meerson. 77, 78)." On adrenaline: "Raising body sensitivity to adrenaline, in the beginning stage of training, leads to extreme mobilization of energy sources during muscular activity. Together with this, according to the amount of increase in trainedness, the sensitivity of the tissues to the adrenaline decreases, this then produces a more economic distribution of the energy resources of the body (Yakovlev, 141, 142)."

**Why it works** — A smaller hormonal surge for the same load is the neuro-humoral level of economy in [[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]]. The adrenaline mechanism is offered as a proposal: "It can be proposed that this mechanism (decrease in the sensitivity of the tissues to adrenaline) conditions function economy, which ensures mobilization of respiration and glycolysis during execution of intensive loads (Pishniak, 100)" (PDF 543).

**When to apply** — Inference: when the same standard session produces a smaller stress response over weeks, that is the expected sign of adaptation, and the standard session has become less of a stimulus.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: cited reviews, no data. The adrenaline link is explicitly "proposed." The page has an internal tension: 1.7 opens by saying economy at the neuro-humoral level comes from "greater reactiveness of the adapted organs to the mediator and hormone actions" (PDF 541 / p.530), while this passage says tissue sensitivity to adrenaline decreases with trainedness. Inference: the two may refer to different organs or hormones; the page does not reconcile them. Inference: a blunted hormonal response can also be a sign of exhaustion (Chapter 8's Addisonic overtraining type, [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]]); this passage does not separate the two.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: "In response to one and the same load in a trained body, there a significant decrease in the activation of the hormonal system" (PDF 543 / p.532).

# Do Not Build Speed by Doing Speed From the Start: Intensify Gradually up to the Main Competitions (Fig 12, Variant B and Curve c)

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.8, "The optimal regime of adaptation" (PDF 544-547 / pp.533-536, checked against the page images). Verkhoshansky first states the view he rejects: "it is logical to assume that speed should be improved with speed work ... In order to develop strength it is necessary to use strength exercises, in order to increase speed it is necessary to execute speed work. This is a natural path for improvement of sports mastery (Moreno, 94). Many coaches follow this outwardly non-controversial logic in practice" (PDF 544 / p.533). He quotes middle and long distance coaches' maxims, among them "it is better to run 100 km a week with a specific speed load than to run 200km at a low intensity" (Verkhoshasky [sic], 26), and notes that many runners "begin to use intense interval and competitive runs even at the beginning of the preparatory period (Nurmekiwi, Piamat, 91)." His verdict: "from two alternative variants, increasing speed or power on the long stage of training (Figure 12, I) coaches usually select variant 'A' and make a big mistake." Early intensification "sharply raises the functional abilities of the athlete and his competitive result. But, it does not create the morpho-functional base for further improving the specific work ability and sports progress. Because of this, such increases are insignificant and do not last very long (Figure 12, II, graphs 'a' and 'b')" (PDF 544). His conclusion: "the most favourable strategy of training is gradual intensification of the training work up to the moment of major starts (Figure 12, II graph 'c')" (PDF 547 / p.536), and "variant 'c' ... corresponds to variant 'B'" (PDF 546 / p.535).

**Why it works** — Fig 12 (PDF 545 / p.534, read from the image; caption: "Two alternative variants of the dynamic of the speed of competition exercise execution (graphic I - A and B) and the possible variants of the intensification of training work (graphic II - a, b, c) during the large training stage"; V is competition speed, W power output, f "the level of the influence of the training loads on the functional state"). In panel I, A rises fast and flattens; B starts lower, rises steadily, crosses A late and ends higher. In panel II, a peaks first and lowest and then falls; b peaks later and higher and then falls; c rises latest and highest and holds near its peak at the right edge. The text's reason is the missing base: intensity raises function before structure has caught up ([[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]]). He calls the resulting bind a contradiction: "speed requires high intensity specialized work, and from the other side, premature intensification of speed has a negative influence on the development of trainability" (PDF 546 / p.535). His resolution: "speed work is necessary in training, as an important (specific) adaptogenic factor. However, speed work can become an effective means of specialized preparation only when the athlete is prepared for it ... maximally intense speed work should be approached gradually and not started earlier than the moment when the locomotor system, the central system of directing the movements, their coordination and mechanisms of energy provision are sufficiently prepared" (PDF 546).

**When to apply** — When planning the preparatory period of a sport with one or two main competitions. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the principle gives a second, performance-based reason for the same gradual progression.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `supported` because the same section describes a two-group experiment that fits it (Dubinin, [[case-study--dubinin-800m-runners-aerobic-vs-intensive-preparation-fig-13]]) and a rowing experiment with significance testing ([[case-study--burlakova-rowers-at-plus-20-vs-plus-30-bpm-eight-weeks]]); Fig 12 itself is a schematic. Verkhoshansky's own case limits it: early intensive preparation (Dubinin's group B) "is more effective in those cases when a high performance level is required for during the entire yearly cycle" (PDF 547 / p.536). Inference: a football season with a game every week is closer to that case than to a single peak; Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Chapter 6 warns against the opposite error, training "conservatively throughout the preparatory stage and the early competitive phase, deliberately avoiding stressful competitive situations" (PDF 326 / p.315; [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]]). Inference: the two passages are not the same claim (competitive-situation exposure there, physiological intensity of speed work here), so this is recorded as a tension, not a contest; both reject an extreme.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: among runners who start intense interval and competitive runs at the beginning of the preparatory period, the early gains are "insignificant and do not last very long" (PDF 544 / p.533), the pattern of curves a and b in Fig 12.

**Related** — [[claim--premature-intensification-harms-heart-mitochondria-and-support-motor-system]], [[heuristic--endurance-intensification-order-threshold-speed-then-glycolytic-heart-volume-then-power]], [[case-study--dubinin-800m-runners-aerobic-vs-intensive-preparation-fig-13]], [[case-study--burlakova-rowers-at-plus-20-vs-plus-30-bpm-eight-weeks]], [[framework--large-training-cycle-local-spp-before-competition-speed-fig-14]], [[case-study--soviet-sprinters-plateau-after-premature-youth-intensification]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]]

# Do Not Build Speed by Doing Speed From the Start: Intensify Gradually up to the Main Competitions (Fig 12, Variant B and Curve c)

Verkhoshansky first states the view he rejects: "it is logical to assume that speed should be improved with speed work ... In order to develop strength it is necessary to use strength exercises, in order to increase speed it is necessary to execute speed work. This is a natural path for improvement of sports mastery (Moreno, 94). Many coaches follow this outwardly non-controversial logic in practice" (PDF 544 / p.533). He quotes middle and long distance coaches' maxims, among them "it is better to run 100 km a week with a specific speed load than to run 200km at a low intensity" (Verkhoshasky [sic], 26), and notes that many runners "begin to use intense interval and competitive runs even at the beginning of the preparatory period (Nurmekiwi, Piamat, 91)." His verdict: "from two alternative variants, increasing speed or power on the long stage of training (Figure 12, I) coaches usually select variant 'A' and make a big mistake." Early intensification "sharply raises the functional abilities of the athlete and his competitive result. But, it does not create the morpho-functional base for further improving the specific work ability and sports progress. Because of this, such increases are insignificant and do not last very long (Figure 12, II, graphs 'a' and 'b')" (PDF 544). His conclusion: "the most favourable strategy of training is gradual intensification of the training work up to the moment of major starts (Figure 12, II graph 'c')" (PDF 547 / p.536), and "variant 'c' ... corresponds to variant 'B'" (PDF 546 / p.535).

**Why it works** — Fig 12 (PDF 545 / p.534, read from the image; caption: "Two alternative variants of the dynamic of the speed of competition exercise execution (graphic I - A and B) and the possible variants of the intensification of training work (graphic II - a, b, c) during the large training stage"; V is competition speed, W power output, f "the level of the influence of the training loads on the functional state"). He calls the resulting bind a contradiction: "speed requires high intensity specialized work, and from the other side, premature intensification of speed has a negative influence on the development of trainability" (PDF 546 / p.535). His resolution: "speed work is necessary in training, as an important (specific) adaptogenic factor. However, speed work can become an effective means of specialized preparation only when the athlete is prepared for it ... maximally intense speed work should be approached gradually and not started earlier than the moment when the locomotor system, the central system of directing the movements, their coordination and mechanisms of energy provision are sufficiently prepared" (PDF 546).

# Premature Intensification Overloads Tendons and Ligaments, Distorts Technique, Strains the Heart and Damages Mitochondria

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's list of what goes wrong when high speed or power comes too early (9.1 §1.8, PDF 544-546 / pp.533-535, checked against the page images):
1. **Speed-strength sports.** "this leads to overload (and in the worst case, to injury) of the support-motor system which includes the ligaments and tendons. It changes the principal details of the biodynamic structure of the movement system, and the picture of its rhythm-tempo," slowing "the morpho-functional specialization process of the body (mainly in the locomotor system) and ... the formation of motor coordination" (PDF 545 / p.534).
2. **Asthenic syndrome.** "premature intensification of speed work in cyclical and team sports, as well as in individual sports, leads to the asthenic syndrome, that is, inadequate reactions defending the body against sharp shifts in the acid-base balance (see the Author's revue, 25)" (PDF 545).
3. **Heart.** "In agreement with many studies carried out even in the 1960's," loads "with high portions of anaerobic energy provision in insufficiently prepared athletes" are tied to "an overload of heart function, and increased hardness of the arterial walls," which "leads to myocardial dystrophy." Observed in rowing (Chagovetz, 129), middle and long distance running (Trushkova, 113; Zorin, 57; Nurmekiwi, 90), swimming (Piyrits, 97), wrestling (Shiyan, 132) and soccer (Kudasheva, 67) (PDF 545).
4. **Mitochondria and recovery.** With "disturbance in the structural integrity of the skeletal muscle mitochondria" their oxidative power falls and the speed held at the anaerobic threshold drops (Mac Dougall et al, 240, 241). "Extreme intensification of training leads to depression of the catabolic and anabolic stages of the general adaptation reaction of the body, which apparently, limits not only energy provision during the time of work, but also in the super-compensation of carbohydrate and plastic reserves" (PDF 545), resulting "in decreased work capacity (Kostina, 65)" and is "dangerous to the athlete's health" (PDF 546 / p.535).

**Why it works** — The page's common thread is that intensity outruns the structures and regulation that have to carry it (PDF 544-545). The mechanism sentences are hedged on the page ("apparently").

**When to apply** — As a reason not to front-load intense anaerobic or maximal-speed work on athletes who are not yet prepared for it, especially after a layoff or for newcomers. Inference: item 1 is the one most relevant to football, where tendon and ligament overload is the practical risk of early high-speed exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: every item is a citation without study details, and "myocardial dystrophy" is a Soviet-era diagnosis whose criteria the page does not give. Footnote 16 (unsigned) defines asthenic syndrome differently from the main text: "asthenia of heart with symptoms of palpitation and shortness of breath resulting from insufficiency of heart and failure of heart to propel" (PDF 545 / p.534), while the text calls it "inadequate reactions defending the body against sharp shifts in the acid-base balance." Inference: the footnote reads as an editorial gloss; quote whichever definition you use with its source. Item 2's "speed of who maintained" sentence is garbled in translation (PDF 545). The harms are tied to "insufficiently prepared" athletes, not to intense work as such.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own sport list for the cardiac finding: rowing, middle and long distance running, swimming, wrestling and soccer (PDF 545 / p.534).

# Dubinin's 800 m Runners: Early Intensive Preparation Led in Winter and Early Summer, Aerobic-First Preparation Led at the Main Competitions (Fig 13)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 547 / p.536, checked against the page image): Fig 13 gives "the data from experimental annual training programs of two groups of high level middle distance runners (Dubinin, 51). In one group, (A) the task was to develop the aerobic sources of energy and to increase running economy. The main portion of the distance methods of running was taken up by running under the anaerobic threshold level. In group B training, the objective was to improve anaerobic sources of energy ... For this, they used more intense training than in group A. preparation for which began even in the first stage of the preparatory period." Result: "athletes using the intense preparation method (group B) had a higher result in the winter and in the first starts of the summer competitive season. However at the beginning of the main starts later on in the season, the athletes in group A came out on a higher level of sports preparation." The Fig 13 caption (PDF 548 / p.537) adds details the text does not: "Dynamics of the sport results in the 800 m running (above) and the training loads parameters (intensive loads - in black, extensive loads - in grey) in the two groups of the female athletes (the experimental group A and the control group B) during the yearly cycle of preparation."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's reading: "intensification of training in the preparatory period does not guarantee achieving high absolute results in the competitive period" (PDF 547). Fig 13, read from the page image (approximate readings): the result axis runs from 2.06 to 1.54 (min.sec), faster upward. Group A's line starts about 2.04 near I, group B's about 2.02; they cross near V at about 2.00; by the right end A is near 1.54 and B near 1.56. Monthly load bars (X to IX, no unit printed, scale 0-300): group B's black intensive share is present from X and runs roughly 40-95 through the year, with totals falling from about 200 in X to about 60 in IX; group A has almost no black until II-IV, then intensive load rises to about 50-80 from VI to IX, while totals stay about 165-290.

**When to apply** — When choosing between an aerobic-first and an intensity-first preparatory period for a sport with a clear main competition. Verkhoshansky's split: group A's method suits "the main meets of the season (as for example the Olympic games or World Championships) for showing the maximum possible ... results"; method B "is more effective in those cases when a high performance level is required for during the entire yearly cycle of preparation (as for example in the Comrade games)" (PDF 547). Inference: the choice depends on the competition calendar, not only on physiology.

**When NOT to apply** — `supported` because the aim, population, conditions and result are described, but no group sizes, statistics or exact times are given. The text and caption differ: the text says "high level middle distance runners," the caption says "female athletes," "800 m," and calls B the control group. "But this variant can be used only by athletes who are most highly qualified" (PDF 547) follows the sentence on method B; Inference: "this variant" most likely means B, but the page does not say. "Comrade games" is a translation; the event is not identified.

**Example** — From the figure: group B is faster from about I to V; group A passes it at about V and is about 0.02 faster at the end of the season (PDF 548 / p.537, approximate image readings).

# Scale Threshold-Pace Volume to the Runner's Own Threshold Speed: From Up to 15% of Distance Work to 35-40%, and Do Not Run Above It (Zorin)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 549 / p.538, checked against the page image) reports an experiment by Zorin (57) whose purpose was "to evaluate the effectiveness of using distance loads on the AT level in the training of long distance runners. Also, to determine the optimal volume of threshold loads taking into consideration the individual levels of preparation of the runners." Findings: "training, with the use of speed loads and individual AT levels (20-30% of the total volume) gives a real increase in AT and sports results in the 5000m run. If with these volumes they use loads going above the individual AT level by 0.2m/sec, it leads to a decrease in the initial AT level and an insignificant increase in the sports result." And "the greatest effect of threshold loads occurs in those cases when their volume corresponds to the level of preparation of the athlete, in which their volume, expressed as a percent of the total volume of running loads, increases according to the increase in the preparation of the athlete." The recommended threshold volumes, as a share of total distance work, by the runner's AT speed:
- 3.6-3.9 m/s: up to 15%.
- 4.0-4.3 m/s: 15-20%.
- 4.4-4.7 m/s: 20-25%.
- 4.8-5.1 m/s: 25-30%.
- 5.2-5.5 m/s: 30-35%.
- "For runners, on a higher level of preparation this volume can reach 40%."

**Why it works** — Inference: the page gives no mechanism; the 0.2 m/s result shows that a small step above threshold turns the load into the anaerobic work the section warns slows aerobic development ("work in the anaerobic zone, as was talked about above, slows down development of aerobic abilities," PDF 549).

**When to apply** — When prescribing threshold work for distance runners or other endurance athletes with a measured threshold speed. Inference: the principle (threshold share rises with the athlete's level, and pace stays at, not above, the individual threshold) can be used even where the running speeds do not fit.

**When NOT to apply** — `supported` for the experiment, whose aim, population and two conditions are described, but no sample size or statistics are given. The five-band table is a recommendation; the page does not show which data it was derived from beyond the 20-30% result. It is for long-distance runners. Inference: in football the baseline's general speed ceiling "around 4.5 m/s" for aerobic work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit) sits inside the 4.4-4.7 m/s band, but that ceiling is a cap for below-threshold work, not a measured threshold speed, so the table does not transfer.

**Example** — Zorin's finding as reported: 20-30% of total volume at the individual AT raised AT and 5000 m results; running the same volume 0.2 m/s above AT lowered the initial AT level (PDF 549 / p.538).

# Intense Training in 1500 m Runners From October to March: Glycolytic Enzymes and Fast-Fibre Size Up, Oxidative Enzymes, Slow-Fibre Size and VO2 Max Down (Neumann, Table 3)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 549 / p.538, checked against the page image): "work in the anaerobic zone, as was talked about above, slows down development of aerobic abilities. As a result, a significant increase in training intensity, of anaerobic functional abilities increase and the aerobic decrease (Table 3)." Table 3, "Influence of intense training in 1500m runners on the functional base of muscle cells and maximum oxygen utilization (G.Neumann, 1990)," as printed (October, March):
- "Productivity of energy exchange in the fast twitch fibers (%)": 10, 20. Then "Glycolytic": 10, 20; "Oxidative": 15, 3.
- "Cross section of muscle fibers (MKM2)": slow twitch 5888, 5312; fast twitch 5856, 6080.
- "Enzyme activeness in FG fibers (millimoles per sec.Kg)": "Citrate synthase (oxidative)" 700, 430; "Phosphogylcerol kinase (glycolytic)" 2550, 3650.
- "Maximum oxygen utilization, ml/kg per min.": 71.0, 67.0.
His conclusion (PDF 550 / p.539): "in the preparatory period when training is directed mainly to the development of aerobic power, the use of such loads should be limited."

**Why it works** — The table shows the shift the text names: glycolytic markers up, oxidative markers down. Inference: in percentage terms citrate synthase fell by about 39% and phosphoglycerate kinase rose by about 43%, slow-fibre area fell about 10% and fast-fibre area rose about 4%, and VO2 max fell 4.0 ml/kg/min (about 6%).

**When to apply** — As a warning that a preparatory period dominated by intense running can trade oxidative capacity for glycolytic capacity in the muscle itself, not only in performance tests. Inference: it is the muscle-level counterpart of the Dubinin result ([[case-study--dubinin-800m-runners-aerobic-vs-intensive-preparation-fig-13]]).

**When NOT to apply** — `supported`: the population (1500 m runners), the condition (intense training), the two time points and the values are printed; the number of runners, the training content and any statistics are not. The first block is hard to read as printed: a row "Productivity of energy exchange in the fast twitch fibers (%)" carries 10 and 20, the same values as the "Glycolytic" row under it, and the "Oxidative" row falls from 15 to 3; Inference: the first row is probably a heading whose values were repeated in error. "MKM2" is a transliteration of square micrometres. There is no control group, so the season itself, not intensity alone, could account for part of the change.

**Example** — From the table: citrate synthase in fast glycolytic fibres fell from 700 to 430 while VO2 max fell from 71.0 to 67.0 ml/kg per min between October and March (PDF 549 / p.538).

# The Large Training Cycle (Fig 14): Block A Local SPP at Moderate Competition Speed, Block B Intensify the Competition Exercise, Block C Compete

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 550 / p.539, checked against the page image) first names the risk of the gradual route: "if a significant portion of time is devoted to execution of the sports events at a moderate speed, then at the moment of major competition there will simply not be enough time to adapt the body to the speed work regime," and "in cyclical and team type sports ... the muscle groups that carry the main load a will remain behind the vegetative systems according to tempo and level of functional improvement" (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25). His answer: "it is expedient at the beginning of the big training cycle, when the competitive exercises are executed at a moderate speed, to selectively intensify the motor system work regime with special physical (including strength) preparation. The exercises should be directed locally to those muscle groups that are mainly involved in competitive conditions. After this, according to the amount of resolution of this task, it follows to use quality intensification of the competitive exercise by gradually increasing execution almost up to maximum speed." The scheme: "A. Means (loads) ensuring morpho-functional specialization of the body as a whole and primarily the locomotor system in correspondence with the specific competitive activity - task of getting ahead with the body preparation for speed work ... B. Means (loads) directed to the intensification of the motor regime, using primarily the competitive exercise. C. Competition activities (loads) with the increasing of speed." Fig 14 (PDF 551 / p.540, read from the image) has three panels over "Basic stage Block A," "Special stage Block B" and "Competition stage Block C." Top: overlapping load humps A, B, C, with the result curve V falling below its start V0 during A and rising through B and C to V1 (the gain marked ΔV). Middle, "TRAINING RUNNING SPEED": a rising curve that starts at "Optimal speed (threshold level - V_OPT)," passes "Training max speed - V_MAX" around the B-C boundary, and approaches "Competition max speed (top speed - V_TOP)" by the end of C. Bottom, "RUNNING LOADS VOLUME": V_OPT volume peaks early in A and declines; V_MAX volume peaks in B; V_TOP volume peaks in C. The caption calls V "the hypothetical trend of sport result."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky: the coach still "intensifies the entire work regime of the body in conditions approaching the competitive," but "thanks to the preliminary morpho-functional preparation of the motor and other physiological systems of the body, this does not lead to its overload" (PDF 550). Inference: block A solves the two problems he names, too little time to adapt to speed and the working muscles lagging the cardiorespiratory systems, by raising the local muscular "motor regime" with SPP while running speed stays moderate.

**When to apply** — When building a year (or a long off-season) toward a target competition period: a local, strength-heavy SPP block first, then progressive speed in the competition exercise, then competition. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming 'compass'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: Fig 14 orders the same qualities across one cycle, with speed held to the late blocks.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Fig 14 is a "principle scheme" and the result curve is labelled "hypothetical"; the page refers to other studies for details (Verkhoshansky, 25, 284, 285; Verkhoshansky, Zaleev, 29). The panels are drawn for running (threshold, training max, competition top speed); the page gives no durations for A, B or C. Inference: the dip in V during block A is the LDTE pattern ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]), so a sport with competitions every week cannot use block A in season.

**Example** — The caption's block A: "stage of the concentrated training loads finalised to the morpho-functional specialization of the body as a whole and primarily the locomotor system in correspondence with the specific competitive activity" (PDF 551 / p.540).

**Related** — [[framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks]] (6.12, no speed work during the strength block), [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]], [[framework--pasm-laws-of-adaptation-to-temporal-forms-of-training-fig-3]]

# Soviet Sprinters Led East German Sprinters at 13-18 but Stalled After 18, Which Galukhin Blamed on Premature Intensification

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky carries the 1.8 argument to multi-year training (9.1 §1.8, PDF 550-552 / pp.539-541, checked against the page images): "All of what has been said above about the optimal regime of development of the adaptational process in the yearly cycle, relates fully to multiyear training. Premature intensification and preparation of young athletes does not create favourable conditions for progress in their future mastery." His example: "in the preparation of sprinters, Soviet coaches for many years were oriented not to creating a solid foundation for achieving high level results, but to fast tempo increases in achievement based on narrow specialized means. This led to early mobilization of reserves possessed by young athletes which exhausted their capabilities and as a result, at 18-20 years of age, to stabilization of results in comparison to stronger foreign athletes (Galukhin, 41, Kniazeva, 63)." The comparison: "at age 13-18 the mean results of the strongest runners in the USSR surpassed those of East German runners and after 18 years of age results of soviet sprinters stabilized and increased insignificantly up to 20-23 years of age when at the same time the East German runners were found to have improved concluding with world class results in the 100 and 200 meters" (PDF 551 / p.540). The cause, "as shown by analysis of the training methods, was in the incorrect distribution of means and methods of training in the process of multiyear planning, which is in the premature intensification of training (Galukhin, 41)." Children's youth sports schools "most frequently used means and methods characteristic of high level sprinters with sufficiently high volumes" (PDF 552 / p.541).

**Why it works** — The counter-finding (Kniazeva, 63; PDF 552 / p.541): "on the beginning stage of sports specialization, improvement in the functional and physical preparation is the base for future mastery. With less intense but more varied exercises, not only was there no decrease in the level of increase in sports results, but it created better conditions for further sports improvement of young runners specializing in the short distances."

**When to apply** — When a young athlete's programme copies an elite one. Eric's baseline: "Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 173, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the page gives a performance reason for the same stance, aimed at the years before college.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: no numbers, sample sizes or training data are given for either country, and the cause is the analysts' attribution. Inference: other differences between the two systems (selection, coaching, and East German doping programmes of that era, which the page does not mention) could explain part of the gap, so the comparison cannot isolate training intensity. Kniazeva's result is stated without design details.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: Soviet sprinters led at 13-18 and "stabilized and increased insignificantly up to 20-23 years of age," while East German sprinters went on to world-class 100 and 200 m results (PDF 551 / p.540).

**Related** — [[heuristic--early-specialisation-by-motor-regime-not-by-sport]], [[claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]], [[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]], [[case-study--junior-sprinters-short-and-long-jump-training-effects]], [[framework--pasm-laws-of-adaptation-to-temporal-forms-of-training-fig-3]]

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky carries the 1.8 argument to multi-year training (9.1 §1.8, PDF 550-552 / pp.539-541, checked against the page images): "All of what has been said above about the optimal regime of development of the adaptational process in the yearly cycle, relates fully to multiyear training. Premature intensification and preparation of young athletes does not create favourable conditions for progress in their future mastery." His example: "in the preparation of sprinters, Soviet coaches for many years were oriented not to creating a solid foundation for achieving high level results, but to fast tempo increases in achievement based on narrow specialized means. This led to early mobilization of reserves possessed by young athletes which exhausted their capabilities and as a result, at 18-20 years of age, to stabilization of results in comparison to stronger foreign athletes (Galukhin, 41, Kniazeva, 63)." The comparison: "at age 13-18 the mean results of the strongest runners in the USSR surpassed those of East German runners and after 18 years of age results of soviet sprinters stabilized and increased insignificantly up to 20-23 years of age when at the same time the East German runners were found to have improved concluding with world class results in the 100 and 200 meters" (PDF 551 / p.540). The cause, "as shown by analysis of the training methods, was in the incorrect distribution of means and methods of training in the process of multiyear planning, which is in the premature intensification of training (Galukhin, 41)."
