# Intense Loads and the Peak of Form Depress Immunity: Illness Rises 5-10 Times in the Competitive Period and up to 25 Times Just Before Competition

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.9, "The phenomena of decreasing of immunological reactivity" (PDF 552-553 / pp.541-542, checked against the page images). Verkhoshansky: "It has long been known that extreme physical and psycho-emotional loads in contemporary sport have a depressing influence on the defense systems of the body (Kassil et al, 61, Surkina et al. 109)." He lists six contributors to "disturbance of immunological homeostasis": "a) increasing imbalance in the humerol-hormonal regulatory function during intense sports loads; b) exhaustion of the sympathoadrenal system and hypophyseal-adrenocortical hystem; c) progressive increases in activeness of the trophotropic mechanisms; d) accompanied increases in tonus of the centrally formed parasympathetic section of the vegetative (autonomic) nervous system; e) increased permeability of the Hematoencephalic barrier for several hormones and; f) deep metabolic changes arising in the middle of the mix (Levando et al., 70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." The numbers: "If illness in athletes before beginning the training year with moderate intensity loads is 1, then in the competitive period tied in with intensified trainings, it increases 5-10 times, and immediately before competition up to 25 times (Levando, 76). It is known that on the day before and during many major competitions, up to 40% of the athletes had an illness that decreased their potential and ability to achieve high results (Levando, 69, Levando et al.70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." And: "at the peak of trainedness in weightlifters, wrestlers and other athletes, there is frequently observed a decrease in resistance to the influence of cold and cold type illness (Meerson, Pshennikova, 78)."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky ties it to intensity, not training as such: in rowers, loads "lead to a decrease in immune reactiveness, and its recovery takes place very slowly. This is tied in with inadequately high intensity of the loads used" (Aronov et al, 2); in children, "an optimal training load in young athletes increases the immunological reactivenss in comparison to children not participating in sport. But, during intense loads, the immune-reactiveness of children decreases (Suharev, Suhanova, 110)" (PDF 552 / p.541).

**When to apply** — When planning the weeks before a main competition and the competitive period: the page puts the highest illness rate exactly where performance matters most. Inference: hygiene and exposure control matter most in the precompetitive week, and a cluster of colds then is a load signal as well as a medical one ([[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: all figures are cited (Levando and others) with no populations, definitions of "illness," or study design. "Levando, 76" uses the reference number that 9.1 elsewhere gives to Meerson (for example "Meerson, 76," PDF 534); the citation may be misnumbered. The six mechanisms are listed, not argued. Footnote 17 (unsigned) defines the "Hematoencephalic barrier" as the blood-brain barrier (PDF 552 / p.541).

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: up to 40% of athletes at many major competitions had an illness on the day before or during the event that lowered their performance (PDF 553 / p.542).

**Related** — [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]], [[heuristic--immune-restoration-is-the-slowest-so-protect-athletes-after-peaks-and-illness]], [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]]

# The Immune System Restores More Slowly Than Other Systems, So the Vulnerable Window Outlasts the Feeling of Recovery; After Serious Illness It Can Take Months

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.9, PDF 553 / p.542, checked against the page image): "The restorative processes in the immune system are, to a significant degree, slower in comparison with other physiological systems. Even if the body was capable of spontaneously restoring its defense functions when it has expressed exhaustion, it requires a greater amount of time during which the body is vulnerable to unfavorable factors (chilling, change in climate or geographic zone, contact with sick individuals and so on). In separate instances (after serious illness, a break in adaptation) the period of restitution can be dragged out over several months, that provokes repeat illnesses. In similar situations athletes practically have to stop training and frequently stop participating in sport (Surkina et al. 109)." The rowing finding on the previous page agrees: immune reactiveness falls and "its recovery takes place very slowly" (Aronov et al, 2; PDF 552 / p.541).

**Why it works** — The page states the time difference but no mechanism. Inference: if performance markers recover faster than immune function, an athlete can look ready while still exposed, which is the risk the page names (chilling, travel, contact with sick people).

**When to apply** — After a peak, a hard competitive block or a serious illness: plan travel, cold exposure and contact with sick people as risks for longer than performance recovery suggests. Inference: in football, the post-season travel and the return after a significant illness are the obvious windows; the page gives no durations for the ordinary case.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: no study or data is described; "several months" refers only to "separate instances (after serious illness, a break in adaptation)." The page gives no way to measure immune recovery. Return to training after illness is a medical decision; this passage does not set criteria.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own list of the risks during the slow window: "chilling, change in climate or geographic zone, contact with sick individuals" (PDF 553 / p.542).

**Related** — [[claim--intense-loads-and-peak-form-depress-immunity-and-raise-illness]], [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]], [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]]

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).

The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.

The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)

**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology). From 9.1: [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]] (9.1, Fig 5).

**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky's own paper uses supercompensation without the 1.16 reservation (both checked against the page images). One of the three bases of the constructive effect is "supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins)" (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519), and by the "rule of V.Engelgard," "in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)" (PDF 533 / p.522). This adds a within-book contradiction to the contest recorded above. See [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] and [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]].

# The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
- specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."

From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).

**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). Inference: the long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block; the page says only that it "is related to the long stages of training" (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and the 1.16 text states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (PDF 99 / p.88; see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is not stated on the page.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).

# Put Technical Training in the Delayed-Effect Window, and Keep Competition-Period Strength Work Short, Intense and Small

**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).

The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).

**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors give no day-level timing.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, "Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis"; PDF p. 515 / printed p. 504, checked against the page image) restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: an "insignificant increase" in specialised strength volume "(by only a few percent)" to "maintain" the achieved level "led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, checked against the page image). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip: its own example fits Chapter 6, and the Addendum is a separate translation of Verkhoshansky's text, which makes a translation slip plausible. The book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376), so the separation is a matter of emphasis.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own, from the Addendum (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image): the text says its Figure 8 shows that "in triple jumpers," concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April were followed by a rise in speed-strength and results in May-June; raising strength volume "by only a few percent" to hold the gain then brought "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results." The page switches from plural to singular here: the volume rise was "as believed by the athlete," and "the athlete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team." Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** the two share the idea that systems
gain and lose adaptation on different timelines, but their orderings conflict: the baseline
has aerobic lost fastest and alactic slowest, while Platonov's reverse order (stated for
overtraining, printed 86) has CP lost first and oxidative/glycogen last. Record this as a
tension, not a convergence.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
three-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist. The source states the reverse-order loss for overtraining,
not for simple layoffs; the entry's own extension to detraining/layoffs beyond what the
text states is this entry's inference, not the authors' claim.

**Example** — Inference: by the stated reverse order, CP-related qualities (gained last)
would be lost first, and oxidative and glycogen qualities lost last. The source states this
reverse order for overtraining, not for a training layoff; it separately notes that longer
training makes the accompanying biochemical changes persist longer after cessation
(printed 86), which is the closest the text comes to describing simple detraining.

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# Skilled Lifters Spend Less Energy per Lift, and Discrete Singles Cost More Than a Continuous Set

**What it is** — Based on Vorobyev's (1978) weightlifting data (Tables 3.10-3.12), energy
expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of
energy expenditure (kJ/min, Table 3.10) rises with bodymass class (from 9.9 kJ/min for
Class I-III lifters in the 56 kg division to 23.0 kJ/min in the >90 kg division) and is
lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport than for Class I-III lifters at
every division except 67.5 kg, where MS is slightly higher (13.1 vs 13.0). Absolute energy
expenditure for a 1RM attempt (kcal, Table 3.12) is generally lower for "elite" lifters than
for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean and jerk, 13.7 kcal
(elite) vs 15.5 kcal (ranked); bench press, 8.4 vs 12.2 kcal. (One exception visible in the
table but not discussed by the authors: front squat runs slightly higher for elite lifters
than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11), the clean and jerk is
the most economical major lift and the press from the rack the most expensive, because its
prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than the large muscle mass used
in the clean and jerk. Separately, and independent of the skill tables: the specific energy
expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with rest between each (an
"interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several repetitions with the same
load; during a strength session lasting 1.5-2.5 hours, actual physical work occupies only
5-12 minutes. The text's own narrative range for Class I-III expenditure ("under 8
kjoules/min in the 56 kg division to over 23 kJ/min in the +110kg division," printed 168)
does not match Table 3.10 itself (I-III is 9.9 at 56 kg, and the table's top bodymass class
is "> 90 kg," not "+110kg"); the mean of 14.8 kJ/min the text gives does match the I-III
row's average. Both as printed; not resolved by the authors. (PDF pp. 179-181, printed pp.
168-170, "3.4.6 Efficiency of Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
directly: continuous-style exercise (as in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training)
relies more heavily on momentum and on elastic energy stored in the tendons between
repetitions, and minimizes the amount of eccentric, starting-strength, and isometric work,
all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
stop. Improving movement efficiency (skill) is described as reducing energy cost for any
level of strength, speed-strength, strength-endurance, or other fitness component; the
authors give no mechanism for why skill specifically lowers per-lift energy cost beyond
this general efficiency claim.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against summing kcal or kJ figures across exercise
types to compare training-session cost, and to expect that the same external load performed
as discrete singles with rest between reps is more metabolically demanding per repetition
than the same reps done continuously. Inference: this bears on cluster-set prescription
(discrete reps with intra-set rest), though the book names no such modern method.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly warn that "a simplistic calculation of
energy expenditure... can be very misleading" because it fails to account for rest
intervals between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions; two
sessions should not be treated as equivalent training stress just because their summed
energy expenditure is similar. The authors also distinguish overload (excessive
intensity/load) from overuse (excessive work output) overtraining: "a workout consisting of
a few maximal attempts may elicit an overload type of overtraining far more readily than a
much longer workout relying on many sets with moderate weights," and overload may come more
from technique that raises stress (force per unit area) than from the training load itself
(printed 170); neither is captured by summed energy expenditure. The skill/bodymass tables
are single-lab, Soviet-era weightlifting data (Vorobyev, 1978) specific to the snatch, clean
and jerk, and their component pulls and presses; they are not established as generalizable
to other lifts or populations.

**Example** — Inference: cluster sets (discrete reps with intra-set rest at a fixed load)
likely impose a higher energy cost per repetition than the same reps performed continuously,
consistent with the 35% figure above, though the book presents no cluster-set experiment
itself.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on this specific angle
(skill-linked lifting economy); flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry on cluster
sets or lifting economy is added.

# Colds and Minor Illness Under Prolonged Heavy Loading Mean Cut the Load and Add General Restoration Now

**What it is** — The authors: "changes in the immune response (as reflected by the presence of colds and other apparently minor sicknesses) which accompany conditions of prolonged stressful loading, indicate the end of the general adaptation syndrome during the period of physical exhaustion, and the immediate need to decrease the loading and increase the amount of general restoration. This change in immune response is not necessarily directly associated with the physical loads, but may also relate strongly to increase in emotional stress, due, for instance, to the impending competitions or any other events involving large changes of psychological state. Timeous intervention is essential whenever the slightest hints of such disruptions in immune status become apparent" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image; the right margin is cut, so "accompany," "period of" and "restoration" are partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — The authors place the immune change at the exhaustion stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome, the point where adaptation reserves are used up (PDF 461; see 1.14 as cited in 8.5). Inference: a cold during a heavy block is then not bad luck but a late marker that the load has outrun adaptation, which is why the response is to cut load rather than train through.

**When to apply** — When an athlete in a long, heavy block (or before a major competition) picks up colds or repeated minor illness, reduce the loading and add general restoration at once, and look at emotional stressors as well as training load. Table 8.3 lists "tendency to headaches, colds, fever blisters" under B-type overtraining (PDF 454 / p.443; see [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]]).

**When NOT to apply** — No data are given; the link to the general adaptation syndrome is the authors' interpretation. A cold can come from exposure alone. Inference: the rule fits when illness coincides with "prolonged stressful loading"; an isolated cold in a light week is weak evidence of overload. Illness management itself belongs to medical staff, which the rule does not replace.

**Example** — The authors' own non-training trigger: immune disruption "may also relate strongly to increase in emotional stress, due, for instance, to the impending competitions" (PDF 461 / p.450). Inference: a run of colds in the week before a rivalry game calls for less load even if the training plan has not changed.

# Keep Event-Specific Training Under Competitive Stress in Both Preparatory and Competitive Phases

**What it is** — The authors say the split of the year into preparatory and competitive phases "creates the false impression that no preparation occurs during the competitive phase and no competition occurs during the preparatory phase" (PDF p. 325-326 / printed p. 314-315, verified against the page images). In team sports or track and field the season is "often so prolonged that this distinction cannot always be applied with such purity," and competitions "may serve as a form of testing, controlled training or specific preparation." Applying specificity means "high intensity sport-specific training under competitive circumstances (known as *event-specific training*) during both the preparatory and competition phases." "It is inadequate to train conservatively throughout the preparatory stage and the early competitive phase, deliberately avoiding stressful competitive situations in an attempt to produce maximal supercompensation with minimum injury by a specific date" (PDF p. 326 / printed p. 315). They add: "It can also be misleading to state categorically that there is a generalised training model for each sport," and call for contingency plans for "injury, loss of motivation, premature stagnation, changes in the rules, changes in the competitive roster, and personal trauma."

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "Part of sport specific preparation is training under conditions which simulate those of the actual event so that one can cope efficiently with the demands of competition" (PDF p. 326 / printed p. 315). No physiological mechanism is given. The same chapter's technique section gives a related observation: low competitive reliability relative to training reliability points to difficulty performing "under conditions of high emotional excitement" (PDF p. 329 / printed p. 318).

**When to apply** — When an off-season plan postpones all competitive or game-like stress until the season. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: in a sport with weekly games, the authors' point argues for keeping competitive-intensity practice in the preparatory period rather than treating the season as the first exposure.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors set no dose for event-specific work and do not say how it should be balanced against injury risk; they only reject avoiding it entirely. For athletes returning from injury, competitive-stress exposure is governed by return-to-play criteria, which this passage does not address (Inference).

**Example** — The authors' own framing: competitions in a prolonged season used "as a form of testing, controlled training or specific preparation" rather than only as targets (PDF p. 326 / printed p. 315).

# Speed Sports: No Speed Work During the Strength Block, Speed Starts as the Delayed Effect Rises, and Glycolytic Loading Has Two Peaks

**What it is** — For "speed sports with a cyclical movement structure" (Fig 6.32b caption, PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372) the authors separate strength and speed more sharply than in speed-strength sports (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; both pages checked against the images):
1. **Speed out of the block.** "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage. However, it is possible during this stage to perfect the athlete's motor skill, which directly determines high speed of movement." That skill is intermuscular coordination with "no tension in the muscle groups which do not directly take part in executing the motor tasks," and "This type of work is quite compatible with the athlete's decreased functional state, provided it is executed in the optimal range of intensity of effort and frequency of movement."
2. **Speed starts with the LDTE.** "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE of strength loading (when the 'State' curve rises above the time axis), together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity."
3. **Two anaerobic-glycolytic peaks.** High competition speed "is determined largely by specific speed-endurance." The glycolytic loading "exhibits two peaks": the first "is timed to end near the conclusion of the stage of concentrated strength loading. Specialised strength means are employed and the objective is to develop special strength-endurance which is primarily of a local nature"; the second "follows the period during which volume of speed work reaches a peak. Distance methods (in cyclic sports) or specialised means and methods (in one-on-one events and team sports) are employed... this type of work should be done in segments of small volume and combined with speed work."
4. **Protect explosive strength.** "Along with the rise in strength-endurance, explosive strength tends to decrease when the second peak of the anaerobic-glycolytic loading occurs. Therefore, in those sports where explosive strength is of great importance, it is necessary to include a sufficiently intensive, small volume of maintenance loading."

Fig 6.32(b), read from the image (PDF p. 383, no numeric scale; read at 400 and 600 dpi): during the shaded strength block, two curves fall below the time axis and climb back above it only after the block ends (they end at Vmax, highest at the right, and at STATE). Two curves rise during the block: one rises steadily and keeps rising (ending at S-E), and one rises to a peak in the latter part of the block (about two thirds to three quarters of the way through), falls after it, then rises to a second hump before easing at the right (ending at An-Gly). That shape matches the text's two glycolytic peaks, the first "timed to end near the conclusion" of the block. One curve starts only at the block's end, rises steeply to a mid-panel peak and then falls back (ending at Speed), matching "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE." The right-edge labels are the only certain curve identities; the assignments above follow each curve through the crossings after the block (Inference), and which of the two below-axis curves ends at Vmax and which at STATE is unclear.

**Why it works** — The authors give the reason for allowing coordination work during the block (it is compatible with a lowered functional state) and for the maintenance dose (explosive strength falls during the second glycolytic peak). They do not explain why speed must be excluded entirely rather than reduced. Inference: it follows from their rule that high-intensity work needs a fresh, not a depressed, functional state ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).

**When to apply** — Cyclic speed sports such as sprinting, and by the authors' mention of "team sports" for the second glycolytic peak, sports where repeated speed matters. Eric's baseline: "For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 116, Explicit, claimed again as Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors program two deliberate glycolytic peaks, which goes further than the baseline; their own caution (small segments combined with speed work, a maintenance dose for explosive strength) is the part that fits the baseline best.

**When NOT to apply** — Speed-strength and complex-technical sports keep some technique and do not separate speed so sharply ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Eric's baseline also says "staff do program it in the off-season" for glycolytic work (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)), so the conflict with line 116 is about in-season emphasis. No volumes, durations or intensities are given for either glycolytic peak.

**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a 200 m sprinter spends a concentrated strength block doing strength-endurance circuits and relaxed technical drills with no sprinting, starts sprint work as the block ends, and adds short speed-endurance runs only after sprint volume has peaked, with a few explosive lifts kept in each week.

# Specialise Children Early by Motor Regime, Not by Sport: A Two-Stage Sport-School Model

**What it is** — The authors apply the convergence principle to youth: "particular consideration was given to the advisability of early specialisation, not in the specific type of sport, but in the specific motor regime involved" (Verkhoshansky 1963, 1972 cited). "orientation of the child to the sport and physical training with the sports means does not begin with specialised exercise to achieve competitive performance standards (which can easily lead to forced training). Instead, it begins with systematic management of the functional perfecting of the body" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295, checked against the page image). The model has two stages:
1. A child who shows "a predisposition to a particular form of athletic activity (e.g. quick reactions, speed of movement, a capacity for speed-strength activities or motor dexterity)" trains "in a group specialising in the appropriate motor regime (the first stage of a children's sport school in Russia)," using "a diversity of elementary motor forms which do not involve specialisation in some specific sport." "Competitions, primarily in team sports, are indispensable elements of such training because they involve those same elementary motor forms."
2. As demands rise, "the teacher will determine the child's predisposition to a specific sport and transfer him to the appropriate sport school for specialised training (the second stage)" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295).
The authors add that schools without this system can adopt it "if these two stages of early sporting preparation are applied systematically in a single school or club" (PDF p. 307 / printed p. 296).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: specialising in a sport too early "can easily lead to forced training," and early training should raise "the body's functional abilities" through broad "elementary motor forms." In the convergence model, early specialisation "is firstly according to ability (but not to the physiological system) and is not related to the motor pattern" (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295). They give no data for the model on these pages.

**When to apply** — Youth programmes and first-year college athletes with a narrow sport background: group by motor regime (speed, speed-strength, dexterity) and use varied elementary movements and team games before sport-specific loading. Eric's baseline: "Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 173, Inferred, transcript). Inference: the authors' model is the upstream fix for the problem the baseline describes; at college age it can only be applied as remediation.

**When NOT to apply** — The basis is the authors' reference to Verkhoshansky's own 1963 and 1972 work and the Russian sport-school structure; no outcome data, ages or durations are given, hence `untested`. The model assumes a teacher can judge "predisposition" reliably, which the text does not test. Inference: Bompa's long-term sequential model in this library ([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]) also delays sport specialisation (generally not before about 14-15 in most sports) and cites three longitudinal studies favouring a multilateral base; the two agree on direction. Bompa's model is multilateral rather than grouped by motor regime, so the authors' first-stage grouping by predisposition is their own addition. It does not address athletes who already specialised.

**Example** — The authors' own: a child showing quick reactions or a capacity for speed-strength activities joins a speed-strength motor-regime group at the first stage of a Russian children's sport school, then is transferred to a specific sport school at the second stage (PDF p. 306 / printed p. 295).

# For Aerobic and Anaerobic Productivity, a Long-Term Delayed Effect Has Been Documented Only After Altitude Training

**What it is** — Under "The Delayed Training Effect and Long Duration Work," the authors state: "With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image). Their evidence:
- **Swimmers (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974).** "significant increases" in "maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactate accumulation." "These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at an altitude of 1700m above sea level, with a peak response taking place about 1 week after the altitude training. All of the athletes in the study improved their results immediately after training at altitude."
- **Skaters (Ivanov 1977).** A 4-minute cycle-ergometer test weekly for 3 weeks at 2250 m, then for 3 weeks at sea level. At altitude, mechanical efficiency fell and oxygen consumption, energy expenditure and lactate rose; back at sea level, "the functional efficiency of the work exceeded the pre-experimental levels as a result of more economical metabolism and a significantly diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP" (same page).
- **Not an altitude case: swimmers under large loads (Susman 1978; no altitude is mentioned).** The authors do not call this an LDTE; they give it after stating that disturbance of homeostasis "can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators" (PDF p. 377). Inference: it is offered as a sea-level example of the dip-and-rebound pattern in non-aerobic measures, not as a documented LDTE in aerobic productivity. Large loads slowed "complex motor reactions," reduced precision of movement patterns and of "tracking a moving object," and lowered work capacity, ECG-assessed cardiovascular state, muscle tonus and adrenal-cortex hormone levels. After loads were reduced and intensity altered, these indicators rose "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the altitude cases: hypobaric conditions gave "a very demanding training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body's homeostasis and subsequent activation of its adaptive processes" (PDF p. 376). For why the LDTE is not seen at sea level, they hedge: if it exists there, the disturbance "will occur at the level of more subtle physiological systems" not detectable by "methods used for assessing the more gross aerobic and anaerobic processes," and "adaptation apparently occurs at deeper cellular and molecular levels (e.g. in the mitochondria and endocrine system)" (Yakovlev 1957, 1974; Viru 1969, 1981; Finogenov 1979), while "disturbance of homeostasis can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators" of the central nervous and neuromuscular systems (PDF pp. 376-377). This is a stated hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism.

**When to apply** — When planning or interpreting altitude camps: the book's one quantified case puts the peak about 1 week after a 3-week stay, with changes lasting more than 4 weeks. When judging a heavy endurance block: the authors point to psycho-physiological and neuromuscular indicators as the place a hidden disturbance may show. Eric's baseline: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a neuromuscular marker of that kind is the sort of indicator the authors suggest, though they name reaction, precision and tracking tasks, not jump tests.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample sizes, controls or statistics for any of the three studies, and the skater study has no non-altitude comparison group in the text. The authors say plainly that the LDTE in sea-level distance training is not documented; do not carry the strength-block LDTE timings ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]) over to aerobic work. The LDTE they do report in cyclic sports (middle-distance running, swimming, skating) follows concentrated strength loading and shows in strength-endurance measures, not in aerobic productivity (PDF p. 374). Inference: altitude camps are rare in American collegiate football, so this entry matters mainly for endurance or Olympic-sport programmes.

**Example** — The authors' own: swimmers after 3 weeks at 1700 m improved immediately, peaked about 1 week after returning, and kept the gains for more than 4 weeks (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974; PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365).

# After Heavy Disturbance, Cut Total Volume and Add General Physical Preparation; the Deeper the Disturbance, the Longer the Restorative Stage

**What it is** — The authors' rule for restorative stages after concentrated loading (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image): "Training organisation which elicits extensive and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis necessitates the inclusion of suitable restorative stages for triggering a compensatory reaction, thereby eliminating inappropriately phased peaking of the various functional indicators and stabilising the body at the new functional level. The general volume of the load should be decreased at this time and General Physical Preparation means should be introduced into training so as to intensify the compensatory reaction. The more extensive and prolonged the disturbance of homeostasis, the longer the restorative stage should be."

Three parts:
1. **Purpose:** trigger the compensatory reaction, prevent the functional indicators from peaking out of phase with each other, and stabilise the new level.
2. **Content:** lower total volume, and bring in General Physical Preparation (GPP) means.
3. **Length:** scaled to the size and duration of the preceding disturbance.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the compensatory model: the gains of a concentrated block appear only after volume falls ("after the volume of loading is decreased, their increase accelerates"; PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). They do not say why GPP intensifies the reaction, and give no data for it.

**When to apply** — Inference: plan the stage after any deliberately heavy block as a change of content, not only a cut in load: lower volume of special means, more general work. Inference: size its length to the block before it, longer after a longer or heavier block. Eric's baseline: "Recovery capacity must be 'earned' by training hard enough first" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' rule is the other half of that statement: once the hard block has been done, the restorative stage is part of the plan.

**When NOT to apply** — No durations are given for the restorative stage here. In 5.3.3 the book gives a 1-3 week latency to gains after 4-8 week concentrated blocks (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294; see [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]), and on the page before this one a 7-10 day pause between blocks and a longer, unspecified recuperation after three blocks (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). Bompa & Haff state a similar scaling rule ("the greater the magnitude and duration of the concentrated loading phase, the more time needed for fatigue to dissipate and performance to improve"), as quoted in [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]; that is agreement on direction, not on a number. Inference: "GPP" here is not defined; the means chosen should still not undo the quality just built.

**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: after a three-week concentrated jump and strength block, a sprinter's next week drops the depth jumps and heavy squats, keeps short sprints, and adds general circuits and aerobic work.

# In the Competition Period, Local Blood Flow to the Working Muscles Rises While VO2 Max Falls, and the Authors Credit Endurance Gains to the Blood Flow

**What it is** — "Recently, haemodynamic factors have been shown to play an important role in the functional specialisation of the body during endurance work" (nine citations). In italics: "The redistribution of blood and an increase in circulation to the working muscles contributes to satisfying the oxygen requirements of the muscles and the removal of anaerobic metabolites." This "Differentiation of the vesicular reaction providing effective redistribution of blood flow" (Inference: "vesicular" is probably meant as "vascular") develops in the competition period "as a result of the extensive aerobic loading executed during the preparatory period." In 25 km road cycling, improved performance came with a fall in VO2 max in the competition period while "peak blood flow to the lower extremities increases," and cardiac output also fell (Stepochkin et al 1970). (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249, verified against the page image.) "OBLA (lactate threshold) and VO2 max levels can change independently": while VO2 max falls somewhat in the competition period, "OBLA can rise" (Zatsiorsky et al 1974; Sirenko 1979; Nurmekivan 1974). In qualified skaters the mean change in VO2 max in the competition period is "5-10%," while local blood flow rises "much more significantly (50-250%)" (Mellenberg 1981). The authors conclude that training effectiveness "does not lie in raising VO2 max, but in enhancing the haemodynamic efficiency of oxygen transport," and that, with the muscles' strength and oxidative qualities, "the redistribution of bloodflow and improved local vesicular reaction are important conditions for developing local muscle endurance." (PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250, verified against the page image.) Because these conditions lessen dependence on VO2 max, the assumed "antagonism in endurance sport between the development of the aerobic and anaerobic mechanisms must be questioned (Mellenberg & Khvan, 1982)" (PDF pp. 260-261 / printed pp. 249-250).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: more blood to the working muscles meets their oxygen need and clears anaerobic metabolites, so less glycolysis is needed, which also explains why VO2 max can fall without harm. They support it by citation; the text gives no figures beyond those above.

**When to apply** — When interpreting in-season test results: a flat or falling VO2 max during the competition period need not mean lost endurance if threshold measures and performance hold. Build the aerobic base in the preparatory period, since the authors credit the competition-period blood-flow change to that loading. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery ... not distance capacity." Tagged **Inferred (transcript)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123). Inference: local blood-flow capacity is a plausible route for that recovery, but the book discusses endurance athletes, not repeat-sprint sports.

**When NOT to apply** — A sentence on the same page is unclear: "blood lactate concentration can increase by some 6% as a result of training, while the VO2 max level increases by only 7% (Williams et al, 1967)" (PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250; the image confirms 6% and 7%). As printed, 7% is larger than 6%, so "only" does not fit; the intended figure or measure (perhaps the lactate threshold rather than lactate concentration) cannot be recovered from the text. Do not cite it. The 50-250% blood-flow range is wide and given without method. The antagonism point is the authors developing an argument across two pages (offered as a possible explanation on p.249, questioned on p.250), not settled.

**Example** — The book's own: 25 km road cyclists whose performance improved while VO2 max and cardiac output fell and leg blood flow rose (Stepochkin et al 1970; PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249).

# Intense Loads and the Peak of Form Depress Immunity: Illness Rises 5-10 Times in the Competitive Period and up to 25 Times Just Before Competition

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.9, "The phenomena of decreasing of immunological reactivity" (PDF 552-553 / pp.541-542, checked against the page images). Verkhoshansky: "It has long been known that extreme physical and psycho-emotional loads in contemporary sport have a depressing influence on the defense systems of the body (Kassil et al, 61, Surkina et al. 109)." He lists six contributors to "disturbance of immunological homeostasis": "a) increasing imbalance in the humerol-hormonal regulatory function during intense sports loads; b) exhaustion of the sympathoadrenal system and hypophyseal-adrenocortical hystem; c) progressive increases in activeness of the trophotropic mechanisms; d) accompanied increases in tonus of the centrally formed parasympathetic section of the vegetative (autonomic) nervous system; e) increased permeability of the Hematoencephalic barrier for several hormones and; f) deep metabolic changes arising in the middle of the mix (Levando et al., 70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." The numbers: "If illness in athletes before beginning the training year with moderate intensity loads is 1, then in the competitive period tied in with intensified trainings, it increases 5-10 times, and immediately before competition up to 25 times (Levando, 76). It is known that on the day before and during many major competitions, up to 40% of the athletes had an illness that decreased their potential and ability to achieve high results (Levando, 69, Levando et al.70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." And: "at the peak of trainedness in weightlifters, wrestlers and other athletes, there is frequently observed a decrease in resistance to the influence of cold and cold type illness (Meerson, Pshennikova, 78)."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky ties it to intensity, not training as such: in rowers, loads "lead to a decrease in immune reactiveness, and its recovery takes place very slowly. This is tied in with inadequately high intensity of the loads used" (Aronov et al, 2); in children, "an optimal training load in young athletes increases the immunological reactivenss in comparison to children not participating in sport. But, during intense loads, the immune-reactiveness of children decreases (Suharev, Suhanova, 110)" (PDF 552 / p.541).

**When to apply** — When planning the weeks before a main competition and the competitive period: the page puts the highest illness rate exactly where performance matters most. Inference: hygiene and exposure control matter most in the precompetitive week, and a cluster of colds then is a load signal as well as a medical one ([[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: all figures are cited (Levando and others) with no populations, definitions of "illness," or study design. "Levando, 76" uses the reference number that 9.1 elsewhere gives to Meerson (for example "Meerson, 76," PDF 534); the citation may be misnumbered. The six mechanisms are listed, not argued. Footnote 17 (unsigned) defines the "Hematoencephalic barrier" as the blood-brain barrier (PDF 552 / p.541).

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: up to 40% of athletes at many major competitions had an illness on the day before or during the event that lowered their performance (PDF 553 / p.542).

# The Conjugate Sequence System: Successive Blocks of Unidirectional Loading, Each Built on the Delayed Effect of the Last

**What it is** — The authors name "two main systems of organising long term training: the concurrent system and the conjugate sequence system" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). The concurrent system is "the parallel training of several motor abilities, such as strength, speed and endurance, over the same period." The conjugate sequence system ("sometimes translated from the Russian as the coupled successive system") "involves successively introducing into the training programme separate, specific means, each of which has a progressively stronger training effect, and coupling them sequentially to create favourable conditions for eliciting the cumulative effect of all the training loads." It usually trains "a carefully chosen sequence of specific motor abilities, each of which is confined largely to a given period," and "It is appropriate to use concentrated loading primarily for enhancing the effectiveness of the SPP (Special Physical Preparation) phase" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292; Verkhoshansky 1978 cited). Two sample sequences (PDF p. 304 / printed p. 293):
- **Speed-endurance** (Fig 5.15, verified against the page image): 1. Aerobic; 2. Mixed anaerobic (ATP-CP and anaerobic glycolysis); 3. High energy phosphagens (ATP-CP); 4. Anaerobic glycolysis. "The block of specialised strength work is concentrated in stage 2, speed work is concentrated mainly in stage 3 and is executed against a background of the long-term delayed training effect of the strength block, and stage 4 is devoted to improving speed-endurance while the general volume of loading is decreased significantly." The figure labels the four stages cardiovascular, strength, speed and speed-endurance, draws them as overlapping humps under a rising "Training Potential" line, and its caption says it is "solely a descriptive scheme, which does not give quantitative details of intensity, volume or timing of loading" and that "there may be a certain amount of overlap of all training stages 1-4."
- **Speed-strength and complex-technique sports:** "1. General development work, 2. Concentrated strength loading, 3. In-depth perfecting of technique against a background of the delayed training effect of the strength block 4. Further perfecting of technique under competitive conditions."

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: for elite athletes the concurrent system "produces only average results," so "To evoke a more powerful training effect in athletes who have already accommodated to high levels of stimulation, it becomes necessary to impose intense phases of uni-directional loading on the body" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). "the 'degree of contrast' in training (i.e. the alternation of means with different beneficial training effects over certain optimal periods) is a factor which enhances the functional responsiveness of the body" (PDF p. 304 / printed p. 293). Each stage is run on "the long-term delayed training effect" of the one before. No physiological mechanism for the delayed effect is given in this section; Chapter 6 treats it (see Related).

**When to apply** — Advanced athletes "who are at a high level of special strength fitness," for whom the authors recommend "primarily a complex system of means for: producing the specific training effect of the complex of means; preserving the magnitude of the training effect," the latter "realised by the sequential replacement of one complex combination of means with another" (PDF p. 304 / printed p. 293). Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming ... "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred). Inference: the speed-strength sequence (general work, concentrated strength, technique on the strength block's delayed effect) is the closest of the two to a football off-season, but the authors give it for "speed-strength and complex-technique types of sport," not team sports.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for lower-level athletes on the authors' own account: research supporting the concurrent system was done on "athletes of lower qualification," in whom "the negative influence of the complex system is not apparent" (PDF p. 303 / printed p. 292). **Contested by Issurin.** The library's summary of Issurin 2016 (*Sports Medicine*, pp. 6-7 and 11) records that Issurin judged the evidence for Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model insufficient for broad use in high-performance combat, team-sport and swimming preparation (the reviewed studies improved some fitness measures but did not report team practice or competition outcomes), and presented the model as suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and restricted where many interacting abilities decide performance (see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]). Issurin 2008 agrees with the authors that concentration is for high-level athletes ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]], PDF 44 / printed 33), so the dispute is over which sports the unidirectional version suits, not over concentration as such. Note also a naming overlap in the text: "complex system" is used for both the concurrent system the authors reject for elites (PDF p. 303) and the "complex system of means" they recommend for qualified athletes (PDF p. 304). The second means a complex of means with one primary emphasis, replaced as a whole over time.

**Example** — The authors' own speed-strength sequence: general development work, then concentrated strength loading, then in-depth technique work "against a background of the delayed training effect of the strength block," then technique under competitive conditions (PDF p. 304 / printed p. 293).

# Start the Next Session When the Previous Session's Protein Synthesis Ends or Begins to Fall, Not Sooner and Not Much Later

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, citing Viru (289, 290, 291) (9.1 §1.5, PDF 532 / p.521, checked against the page image): "it is important to give attention to the need for determining the best time (moment) for the repeat work, in relation to the time of development of the post training protein synthesis. In other words, each following training session (or training load portion) must be started only at the moment when the protein synthesis, ensured by the preceding training session, is finished, or when the intensity of this protein syntheses start to decrease. If the following training session is carried out sooner (or too late), the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session will not by realized" (printed so; the sense is "be realized"). He presents this, with the case against restoration procedures and complex loads, as grounds to "review the obsolete principles of training load organization in microcycle coming from the conception of Periodization of Training, introduced by L.Matveev, and working out contemporary models of programming the microcycle" (PDF 532 / p.521).

**Why it works** — The rest interval exists "mainly for realization of the after work specific protein synthesis" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). Inference: load again while synthesis is still rising and the new breakdown cuts it short; wait until long after it has ended and the after-effects that link sessions, which last "several tens of hours" (PDF 531), have faded.

**When to apply** — When spacing sessions that load the same structures or quality, such as two heavy lower-body days or two speed-endurance sessions in a week. Inference: Fig 5 on PDF 533 (animal stress data, not training) shows protein synthesis peaking at about 24 and falling back toward baseline by 120-168 on its time axis (see [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]); if that axis is hours, it would put the next hard session for the same tissues somewhere after the first day and well before a week. The page itself gives no hours.

**When NOT to apply** — No time windows, no measures and no data are given, and protein synthesis cannot be read in the field, so the rule needs a proxy that the page does not supply. It also says nothing about sessions aimed at different qualities, which load different proteins (see [[claim--training-direction-sets-which-proteins-are-synthesised-table-1]]). Rated `untested`. Inference: in an in-season football week the game fixes most of the spacing, so the rule matters most in the off-season.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own failure case: a session "carried out sooner (or too late)" than the end or decline of the previous session's synthesis loses "the main part of the positive influence of the preceding training session" (PDF 532 / p.521).

Batch 9b is written: 24 new entries plus cross-links in 15 existing entries. Lint finds nothing in my files.

- **Batch:** 9b, section 9.1 (middle part), PDF 534-553 / p.523-542. It starts at "Even before this it had been shown…" on PDF 534. The paragraph ending "(Meerson, 76)" was left to 9a.
- **Entries written:** 24.
  - By kind: 9 claim, 6 framework, 5 case-study, 3 heuristic, 1 principle.
  - By confidence: 6 supported (the Fig 8, Dubinin Fig 13, Burlakova and Neumann Table 3 case studies, the Zorin heuristic, and the Fig 12 principle), 18 untested, 0 contested, 0 proven.
- **Contested:** none. I recorded one tension instead of a contest. 6.1 says don't avoid competitive stress in preparation; 9.1 says don't intensify speed work early. They are not the same claim, and each rejects an extreme. Both entries carry locators and reciprocal links.
- **Cross-links:**
  - 10 existing entries got "Also in 9.1" text: 8 new lines, and 2 existing lines extended (adaptive-reconstruction and the 6.10 LDTE principle).
  - 5 more got a Related link only. Two of those are in 9a files: two-levels and start-the-next-session. Each got a single appended link and nothing else.
  - All other links from the new entries to existing entries are one-way.
- **Scope file:** `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_scope_supertraining_ch9b.txt`. It lists the 24 new files, a blank line, then the 15 cross-linked files.
- **`_book.md`:** I added a "9.1 (part b)" row after part a. It is set to done with 24 entries and notes it covers PDF 534-553 only.
- **Exact end point:** PDF 553 / p.542, the last sentence of §1.9: "In similar situations athletes practically have to stop training and frequently stop participating in sport (Surkina et al. 109)."
- **Boundary moved:** yes, by a few lines. §1.10 ("General schematic of the adaptational process during sports activity") starts lower on PDF 553, and its first paragraph runs mid-sentence onto PDF 554, with Fig 15 on 554. So 9c should start at the 1.10 heading on PDF 553.
- **Unreadable pages:** none. Every page was rendered at 150 dpi, and Fig 8 also at 300 dpi.
  - On PDF 536 / p.525 the scan clips the left margin. That hides the list digits 3-6 and the first letters of five lines. The Fig 8 quote from those lines is marked "partly reconstructed", and so is the six-point list numbering in the LDTE cross-link line.
  - The existing 6.10 heuristic quotes those same clipped lines without that flag. I did not edit it.
- **Lint:** 0 issues in my files. The only remaining hits are three em dashes in `_book.md` that were there before (lines 12, 173 and 174). Lines 173 and 174 moved down one because of the new row; they are not new.
